t.roztochya@50.0,23.6:
Roztochia is a low, wooded ridge that runs like a spine from southeastern Poland down to the outskirts of Lviv, and on its Ukrainian end, between Ivano-Frankove and Novoyavorivsk, lies the Roztochia nature reserve. Its old beech woods were added in 2017 to the UNESCO listing of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a chain of forests that tells the story of how beech recolonised the continent after the Ice Age. The ridge is also a watershed: rain that falls on one side ends up in the Baltic by way of the Vistula, and on the other in the Black Sea by way of the Dniester. Standing on a hilltop and knowing that is oddly satisfying.

The country is soft and mixed: sandy soils, pine stands, beech and oak on the slopes, small lakes, fishponds and meadows full of storks in summer. Ivano-Frankove, an old town named after the poet Ivan Franko, sits on a lake, and the woods around it have long been a place for Lviv people to walk, pick mushrooms and swim. Lviv itself, half an hour away, has an old town of Renaissance and baroque streets and the Vysokyi Zamok hill with its view over the roofs.

We should be straight about the present. Ukraine has been under martial law since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, the large Yavoriv military range lies nearby, and travel rules, curfews and checkpoints can change at short notice. Check official advice before planning a ride here and follow local instructions to the letter.

If and when you do ride, the roads west of Lviv are a mixed bag: some main routes are freshly resurfaced, others patched and potholed, and village lanes may be cobbled or sandy. Traffic is a mix of fast cars, trucks heading to the Polish border at Krakovets and horse carts. Novoyavorivsk, six kilometres away, is a town of nearly thirty thousand with fuel and shops; Lviv has everything. Look for varenyky and borscht in roadside cafés, and in Lviv, where coffee culture runs deep, take your time over a cup.
t.potelych tserkva of the descent of the h:
In the village of Potelych, in western Ukraine near the Polish border, a wooden church has stood since the early sixteenth century. The Church of the Descent of the Holy Spirit is one of the oldest wooden churches in Ukraine, built of logs with a tall roof covered in shingles, and its interior holds wall paintings and an iconostasis from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, inscribed in 2013.

The wooden churches of this region were built by Orthodox and Greek Catholic communities, using local timber and building traditions passed down through generations. They have a distinctive shape, with three parts, each topped by a roof or dome, and the interiors are often painted with scenes from the Bible. Potelych was once a town known for its pottery, and the church was built with funds from the local community. The surrounding landscape of Roztochia is one of rolling hills, forests and farmland, straddling the border between Ukraine and Poland.

Travel in Ukraine is currently affected by the war that began with the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, and many governments advise against all travel to the country. If and when travel becomes possible, the roads in this region are generally paved but can be rough, with potholes, and traffic includes trucks heading to the Polish border. The landscape is gentle and green, with villages and forests. Before considering any trip, check the latest travel advice and conditions carefully.

Rava-Ruska, six kilometres away, is a town with fuel and shops, and Lviv, the main city of western Ukraine, is about fifty kilometres south-east. On the Polish side of the border, the wooden churches of the same UNESCO site, such as Chotyniec and Radruż, can be visited more easily. Ukrainian food is hearty: borscht, varenyky, dumplings filled with potato or cheese, and holubtsi, cabbage rolls. The church at Potelych, with its dark wood weathered by five centuries of sun, rain and snow, is a powerful symbol of endurance.
t.saltworks castle in wieliczka@50.0,20.1:
Wieliczka is a town that sits on top of a vanished sea. Millions of years ago, this part of southern Poland lay under a shallow, salty basin, and as the water evaporated it left thick beds of rock salt, which people have mined for about seven hundred years. The Saltworks Castle, the Żupny Castle, was the administrative heart of the business, a medieval fortified complex that housed the managers, the accounts and the royal officers who ran one of the richest enterprises in Poland, since salt was money. For centuries the revenue from Wieliczka and neighbouring Bochnia paid a significant share of the Crown's expenses.

The mine below is one of the great sights of Europe. Visitors walk down several hundred steps, through timbered shafts and long galleries, to chambers carved by miners, including St Kinga's Chapel, a cathedral-sized space where the chandeliers, altars, floors and relief carvings are all made of salt. It was among the first twelve sites placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1978. The air is cool and slightly salty, and the guide will tell stories about miners, horses and underground lakes. The tourist route takes a couple of hours and covers only a small part of the mine, and a lift brings you back to the surface.

Wieliczka lies right next to Kraków, so riding here is mostly about reaching it from the city. The roads on the southern edge of Kraków are busy, with trams, buses and a lot of traffic, so go early or avoid weekends in summer, when the mine is full of coach parties. Fuel, food and parking are easy in a town of nearly nineteen thousand, and there are cafes on the market square.

The better riding is south of town, where the land rises toward the Beskids, with rolling farmland, orchards and small villages along the roads, and further south the foothills have good winding sections. The second part of this ride goes to Powroźnik, in the south of Małopolska, with its wooden Orthodox church, built by the Lemko people, a mountain community with its own culture and its own style of church, with onion domes in wood. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and winter is cold but dry. Eat a hearty soup, a plate of pierogi and an apple cake, and ask the guides which direction the old sea went.
t.chotyniec tserkva of the birth of the bl:
Out on the flat, open country east of the San river, close to the Ukrainian border, stands a wooden church that has been watching the fields for more than four hundred years. The Church of the Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Chotyniec dates from the early seventeenth century and belongs to the eastern tradition of Christian building in this borderland, where Ruthenian communities worshipped in the Greek rite. It is one of the churches listed together as the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region, and it has a tall, three-part design, with a nave, a smaller chancel and a bell tower, each topped by a wooden cupola.

Inside, the focus is on the iconostasis, the screen of icons that divides the sanctuary from the nave, which is the main glory of the church. The paintings, in rich reds, golds and blues, are of saints and biblical scenes, and the effect is dimly glowing. If the church is closed, ask in the village for the person who holds the key. The graveyard around it, with its old crosses and quiet atmosphere, belongs to a long story of mixed populations, shifting borders and wartime upheavals, and it is respectful to keep voices low.

The landscape is gently rolling farmland, with fields of wheat and maize, orchards, small woods and low ridgelines. It is not dramatic riding, but it is pleasant, with straight roads, light traffic and easy bends. Roads are generally good, though small village lanes can have rough patches. The best time is early summer, when the fields are bright, or September, when the harvest is in and the air is clear. In winter, the plains can be cold and windy.

Radymno, on the San river, is the closest town of any size, with fuel and shops, and Jaroslaw to the west is larger still. Villages such as Stubno and Laszki have a small shop at best. This is a quiet corner of the country, and the reward is a sense of space, farm smells, storks on the chimneys in summer, and the plain beauty of a building made entirely of wood and patience.
t.old city of zamosc@50.7,23.3:
Zamość is a town that was designed on a drawing board, and it shows. In 1580 the chancellor Jan Zamoyski, one of the richest men in Poland, hired an Italian architect from Padua, Bernardo Morando, to build an ideal Renaissance city on his own estate. The plan was strict and elegant, with a central square, a regular grid of streets, a palace, a cathedral, an academy and a ring of bastioned fortifications, and the town was meant to be a trading centre on the road between Lublin and Lviv. People called it the Padua of the North, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1992.

The Great Market Square is the heart. It is exactly one hundred metres on each side, framed by arcaded merchants' houses in pastel colours, with a tall town hall on the north side and a double flight of curved stairs added in the eighteenth century. Armenian merchants settled here in the early years and built their own houses on the square with decorated attics, and their family arms and ornate parapets give the arcades their individual character. The cathedral, a short walk away, holds the Zamoyski tombs, and the fortifications, though partly rebuilt after the Russian army took them down in the nineteenth century, still enclose the old town.

The ride in is straightforward. Zamość lies on the Roztocze, a ridge of low forested hills in south-east Poland, and the roads from the north and south run through rolling farmland, beech and pine woods, and small villages with wooden houses. The surface is generally good, although some minor roads are patchy, and the traffic is moderate. The Roztocze National Park, a short ride to the south, has forests of fir and beech, and a herd of Polish konik horses, a small hardy breed descended from wild tarpans.

Zamość is a city of about sixty-six thousand people, so fuel and meals are easy to find. Park outside the old town, and walk in through the gates. On a warm evening the square fills with tables and the colours of the facades glow in the last light. Try pierogi, a bowl of hot barszcz, or a local beer, and give yourself time to circle the square slowly, looking up.
t.salt mine in wieliczka@50.0,20.1:
For more than seven hundred years, miners dug salt out of the ground at Wieliczka, and when they stopped selling it in 2007 they were still at it. The deposit is a gift of an ancient sea, a salt layer laid down some thirteen million years ago in the Miocene, and when the Polish kings came upon it, in the Middle Ages, salt was as good as money. At one stage the mine provided a large share of the royal revenue, and Kraków became rich on the proceeds. The mine now reaches over three hundred metres deep, with hundreds of kilometres of tunnels, and was one of the first twelve sites ever put on the UNESCO World Heritage list, in 1978.

The visitors' route, around three kilometres long, goes down hundreds of wooden steps and through galleries lined with timber props, with statues, chambers and an underground lake, all carved out of salt. The famous highlight is the chapel of St Kinga, a full-sized underground church about a hundred metres below the surface, whose chandeliers, altars, reliefs and floor are all carved out of salt by miners over decades. According to the legend, Kinga, a Hungarian princess who married a Polish prince, threw her engagement ring into a salt mine in Hungary, and it was found in the first block of salt dug at Wieliczka. Many visitors lick the walls, to check, and the guides smile.

The town of Wieliczka, with about eighteen thousand people, sits just southeast of Kraków, and fuel, food and parking are easy. The ride from Kraków is only a quarter of an hour, but the city deserves a day of its own, with Wawel castle, the old market square and Kazimierz, the old Jewish quarter. South of the mine, the country rises into the foothills of the Beskids, where roads wind through villages and forests with old wooden churches, and good riding begins within an hour.

Be prepared for crowds in summer and book tickets ahead. The mine stays at a steady temperature of around fourteen degrees, so a jumper is wise, even in July.

Try a bowl of zurek, the sour rye soup, and a plate of pierogi, ideally after a morning underground.
t.kaunas@54.9,23.9:
Kaunas sits where Lithuania's two greatest rivers, the Nemunas and the Neris, meet, and that gives the city its shape: an old town on a tongue of land between the waters, a newer town running east along a long straight pedestrian avenue, Laisvės alėja, and green hills on every side. Between the two world wars, when Vilnius was held by Poland, Kaunas served as the provisional capital of independent Lithuania, and in those twenty years it filled with ambitious modernist buildings, whose white, clean lines have now been recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage site.

The old town has a quieter charm. The brick castle, with its stout tower, guards the confluence, and the town hall, nicknamed the white swan, rises above the square with its tiered white tower. Just outside the centre, the Pažaislis monastery, a baroque masterpiece in white stone on the shore of the Kaunas Reservoir, was built in the seventeenth century and has a fine fresco-covered interior. The city also has a mixed, sometimes painful past, and the Ninth Fort, a former tsarist fortress that became a site of mass killing during the Nazi occupation, is a sober place to visit.

As a starting point for riding, it is easy. The A1 motorway leads east to Vilnius, about a hundred kilometres away, and the road is fast and smooth, with long straights through forest and farmland. Smaller roads alongside the Nemunas, however, are more attractive, running through pine woods, past villages with wooden houses, and over low hills that give a modest sense of curve. Lithuania is a gentle country, with its highest point only about three hundred metres, and the pleasures are in the light, the lakes and the forests rather than in dramatic bends. Summer evenings are very long, and in June it hardly gets dark. Winters are cold and snowy, so most riding takes place between May and September.

Food is hearty. Cepelinai, huge potato dumplings stuffed with meat and served with sour cream and bacon, are the national dish, and cold beetroot soup, šaltibarščiai, a vivid pink, is welcome on hot days. A strong dark rye bread and a glass of local beer round it out. Fuel is easily found everywhere in the city and along the main roads, and the suburbs of Aleksotas and Šilainiai have supermarkets and stations. Speed limits are enforced, and headlights must be on at all times in Lithuania.
t.trakai@54.6,24.9:
Lithuanians hold up Trakai the way the French hold up Mont-Saint-Michel. A red-brick castle with a tall keep stands on an island in Lake Galvė, joined to the shore by a wooden bridge, with reeds, water lilies and sailing boats all around it. It was built in the fourteenth century by the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, then a pagan power that spread across much of what is now Belarus and Ukraine, and the dukes Kęstutis and Vytautas made it a key seat of their power. Vytautas the Great, the most celebrated medieval ruler of Lithuania, is said to have died here in 1430. After centuries of decay the castle was largely rebuilt in the twentieth century.

The town is also interesting for its people. Vytautas brought a group of Karaites, a Turkic-speaking community of Jewish faith, to Trakai around the year 1400 to serve as guards, and a small community still lives here, with colourful wooden houses with three windows on the street, one for God, one for the family and one for the Grand Duke. Their culinary legacy is the kibinai, a crescent-shaped pastry filled with minced meat and onion, served hot in small restaurants all around the shore. Eat one and you will understand why the town is so proud.

For a motorcyclist, Trakai is a gentle outing and an easy day from Vilnius, about thirty kilometres away. The road runs through a landscape of lakes, small hills and pine woods, part of the Trakai Historical National Park, which holds more than two hundred lakes. The surface is generally good, bends are soft and the villages are quiet. This is not mountain riding, but it is easy and pretty, and on a summer evening, when the light turns golden and the water goes still, it is a pleasure. Weekends in summer bring crowds to the castle and the lake, with cars crawling along the shore, so a weekday morning is better. The cold months are quiet, and the lakes freeze, with ice fishermen out on the surface.

Trakai has a population of around five and a half thousand, so fuel, cafes and shops are available in the town, and the larger town of Lentvaris is a few kilometres away. Parking near the castle is limited. Wear sensible shoes for the wooden bridge, and give yourself time to walk the shoreline path, which gives the best views of the castle reflected in the water. Remember that in Lithuania headlights must be on at all times, and speed limits in villages are strictly enforced.
t.tokyo kanto rides@35.2,140.2:
Chiba prefecture is the thumb of land that sticks into the Pacific east of Tokyo, and its southern end is lower, softer and far more rural than most visitors expect, with ridges of forested hills, small rice valleys and a long coast of surf beaches. Katsuura, with twenty-two thousand people, and Ōhara and Kamogawa, both a little further along the coast, are the main towns.

The market at Katsuura has been held on the streets near the harbour since the sixteenth century, and in the early morning stalls sell fish, vegetables, dried goods and pickles, while locals eat the local tantanmen, a spicy sesame-and-chilli noodle soup invented to warm up fishermen. Ōhara is known for its autumn festival, in which men carry heavy portable shrines into the surf, and in the hills nearby, the Yōrō valley offers waterfalls and forest walks. Kamogawa, on the south coast, has a famous aquarium with orcas and dolphins.

For riders, the Bōsō hills are a surprise. The roads are narrow, winding and often empty, with short, steep climbs, hairpins in the cedar woods and sudden views of the sea. The surface is generally good, but leaf litter and damp make shaded corners slippery, and in summer the humidity is intense. The weather here is mild, and the peninsula stays green and warm when Tokyo is cold, with winter camellias and early spring flowers along the coast. Typhoons can bring heavy rain in late summer and autumn, so check the forecast.

Rip currents are a real danger, so swim only where lifeguards are on duty, and be careful of waves. Fuel and food are plentiful along the coast, with seafood the speciality: fresh sashimi, grilled fish and, in a few fishing ports on the southern tip, whale, a local tradition.

The label says Tokyo and Kantō rides, a broad title for what is a rather quiet and little-visited corner. Begin early, take the hill roads, and finish with a bowl of noodles by the sea.
t.sendai@38.3,140.9:
Sendai is the biggest city in Tohoku, the north-east of Honshu, with about a million people, and it wears its history lightly under a mantle of trees. The nickname is the City of Trees, because of the rows of zelkova that line its main avenues, rustling in summer and strung with thousands of lights in winter. Date Masamune, the one-eyed warlord who founded the city in 1601, chose the site on the Hirose river, and his statue sits on the stone walls of Aoba Castle, looking out over the city.

Masamune was a man of taste and ambition, famous for his dramatic helmet with a crescent moon and for sending an envoy to Europe in the early seventeenth century. His mausoleum, Zuihoden, sits in the forest on a hill outside the city, a colourful hall in black and gold. Sendai's best-known food is gyutan, grilled beef tongue, served with barley rice and oxtail soup. The Tanabata festival in early August fills the arcades with enormous streamers of paper.

The city also carries the memory of the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, which devastated the coast just to the east. Sendai's coastal plain was swept by the wave, and the area has been rebuilt with new sea defences and memorial sites, and there are museums and quiet places of remembrance. The nearby bay of Matsushima, dotted with pine-covered islets, was protected by the islands and is among the classic views of Japan.

For a rider, the city itself is easy, with fuel everywhere and good roads. The mountains to the west, such as the Zao range with its volcanic crater lake, the Okama, and the Shiroishi area offer rewarding rides. Spring brings late cherry blossoms, summer is mild, and autumn colours in the hills are glorious. Winter brings snow and closures at altitude. Eat tongue, drink sake and leave time for the castle view at sunset.
t.motsu ji@39.0,141.1:
Motsu-ji is what remains of a great temple in Hiraizumi, in Iwate prefecture, where a powerful family built a Buddhist paradise in the twelfth century. The Northern Fujiwara ruled the far north from here for about a hundred years, rich on gold from the mountains and horses and trade with the north, and they wanted to make a capital to rival Kyoto. Hiraizumi is the heritage that survived, and UNESCO inscribed it in 2011. Ichinoseki, the nearest city, is a few kilometres south.

Motsu-ji is mostly a garden now. The great halls burned down centuries ago, but the lake and its islands survive, one of the best-preserved Pure Land gardens in Japan, designed to represent paradise on earth, with a shoreline of rocks and a reconstructed path. Foundations of buildings show where the halls stood. In early summer the iris garden blooms, and in late August the lake hosts a festival with poetry floating on a stream, a courtly pastime from the Heian court.

The poet Basho came through in 1689 on his journey in the narrow road to the deep north, and wrote one of his best-known verses about the summer grass as all that remains of warriors' dreams. That feeling is exactly right at Motsu-ji. Nearby Chuson-ji, on a wooded ridge, has the Golden Hall, covered in gold leaf, and the whole place has a mood of calm, elegant melancholy.

Riding here is gentle. Roads through the Kitakami river valley are flat and straight, with rice fields and low mountains, and traffic is light. Fuel and food are easy in Ichinoseki and Hiraizumi, and the area is known for mochi dishes, served in many forms. Winter brings snow, and the best seasons are late spring and autumn. Park near the site and walk, since there is no need to rush.
t.kanjizaio in ato@39.0,141.1:
Of all the buildings that once stood in Hiraizumi, Kanjizaio-in is one of the quietest. Only the ruins survive, a pond and a pattern of foundations beside the larger garden of Motsu-ji, but together they give a sense of the scale of the twelfth-century city. The temple was built by the wife of Fujiwara no Motohira, the second lord of the Northern Fujiwara, and the pond was designed to resemble a Pure Land paradise.

The garden has been excavated and partly restored, with a lake whose shoreline was shaped to look natural, a small island and a causeway. In spring the water reflects the new green of the trees, and in autumn the maples turn red around the edge. The old paths through the grass are marked and you can walk around, with signs explaining where the halls, the bridge and the bell tower stood. The site is shaded and quiet, even when the main attractions are busy, and you will often have a bench to yourself.

The Fujiwara rise and fall are the backdrop. They governed from Hiraizumi for four generations, until Minamoto no Yoritomo, the first shogun, attacked in 1189 and the capital burned. Fire and later neglect did the rest, and what survived is the memory in the gardens, along with the gold hall at Chuson-ji. The story has a classic shape: wealth, art, then conquest and silence.

The roads around Hiraizumi are quiet and rural, passing between rice paddies and small farms, with views of low forested hills. Ichinoseki is the nearest city for fuel, food and lodging. Weather is cool and clear in autumn and the snow starts in December. Mornings are best for the light and fewer visitors. A walk here is not strenuous, but a rider in jacket and boots will want to take it slowly and enjoy being off the road.
t.mt kinkeisan@39.0,141.1:
Kinkeisan, the Golden Chicken Mountain, is not much of a mountain, just a wooded hill rising at the edge of Hiraizumi, but it was important enough to the Northern Fujiwara that they buried a sutra on its summit. In 1124 or thereabouts, according to tradition, a sacred text was placed in a bronze cylinder and buried here, with a golden figure of a chicken said to guard it, and that gave the hill its name. A small shrine marks the top, among tall cedars.

From the summit, on a clear day, you look over the paddies of the Kitakami valley and across to Chuson-ji's ridge and the rest of the old capital's scattered remains. The hill sits in the line of the old city, with the original axis of Hiraizumi pointing toward it, so the Fujiwara seem to have designed their paradise around it. Ancient hiking paths wind up through the forest, steeper than you expect, with stone steps worn by pilgrims. Moss and ferns cover the rocks.

The Fujiwara story is why this matters. Their wealth came from gold in the northern mountains and from trade in horses and furs, and their rulers, Kiyohira, Motohira and Hidehira, built a city of temples, pagodas and gardens that rivalled the capital. The family sheltered the famous young warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune, and when his brother Yoritomo, the shogun, demanded him, the Fujiwara hesitated and then fell. The relics of the city that remain, the golden hall and gardens, are the survivors of that fall.

Ichinoseki is the nearest town of size, about nine kilometres off, and has fuel, restaurants and hotels. There is little at the foot of the hill itself, so expect quiet. Visit early in the morning when birdsong fills the woods. Autumn colours light up the slope, and in winter snow covers the paths, making steps slippery. Wear shoes you can walk in, and leave helmets locked to the bike.
t.leakey@29.7,-99.8:
A town of about four hundred people is hardly the likely centre of anything, but Leakey is where Texas motorcyclists come to get their kicks. It sits on the Frio River in the Hill Country, in the little county of Real, among limestone bluffs, bald cypress and live oaks, and it is the base for the roads known as the Twisted Sisters, three ranch roads numbered 335, 336 and 337 that tangle through the hills west of the highway. They are among the most famous motorcycle roads in the state.

The roads climb and fall through the rocky hills and canyons in a long series of tight bends, short straights and steep crests, with views over the Nueces and Frio valleys. The surface can be rough in places, with cattle guards, low-water crossings and loose gravel, and wildlife is a real hazard, since deer, goats and cattle wander onto the road. Weekends bring crowds of riders, and law enforcement is active, so speed limits are worth respecting. Spring, when the hills are covered in bluebonnets and other wildflowers, is the best season, and autumn is also good. Summer is hot, but the clear river water is a good place to cool off.

The Frio is a spring-fed stream with water so clear you can see the pebbles, and swimming at the river parks is a Texas tradition. Garner State Park, a short ride south, is known for its summer dances at the pavilion, where a jukebox has played for generations. To the north, Lost Maples State Natural Area is known for the bigtooth maples that turn red in November, a rare sight in Texas.

Leakey is small, and fuel may be limited, so fill up in a larger town such as Kerrville or Uvalde, each about an hour away. A few cafes and general stores serve burgers and pie, and motels and cabins book out early on busy weekends. Carry water in the heat, and stay alert on blind crests.
t.okutama and@35.7,140.0:
Pears are the local pride. This part of Chiba, east of Tokyo, has been growing Japanese pears since the Edo period, and the orchards of Ichikawa, Matsudo and Funabashi are among the oldest in the country, with roadside stalls selling fruit in late summer.

For a ride that began in the Okutama and Chichibu mountains, it is a long way from the hills. The roads here are straight and busy, with traffic lights and roundabouts, and the surface is good. Route 16 and the Hokusō railway line cross the area, and Narita airport is thirty kilometres to the east, which means occasional aircraft overhead. The best riding is in early morning or late evening, when the traffic is thin and the autumn light is soft.

The plateau has a quiet history. In the Edo period, the government kept horses on pasture land here, the Maki, and the long tradition of horse breeding gave Chiba a link to racing that continues at Nakayama racecourse in Funabashi. The soil is a fine volcanic loam, good for vegetables, peanuts and fruit, and small farms still cultivate it between the houses. A few old shrines and temples, with big trees, stand in hollows and provide some shade.

Fuel and food are easy, with stations on every main road and family restaurants and convenience stores everywhere. In the pear season, from August to October, farm stands sell fresh fruit, and the juice and ice cream are good. The area also has small noodle shops and bakeries, and the local peanuts are boiled or roasted.

Buy a pear and eat it on the roadside. It is cold, juicy and sweet, and a fine way to celebrate the end of the ride.
t.bandai@35.7,140.0:
The city has more than half a million people, and the district here is a mix of apartment blocks, shops and small parks, with the bay a few kilometres to the south. Nakayama racecourse, home of the Arima Kinen, one of Japan's biggest horse races, lies a short way to the north-west.

The ride that ends here has crossed the Bandai-Azuma mountains, so this is a long step down. The roads are busy, flat and full of lights, and the surface is good. The expressway along the bay carries heavy traffic, and the Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line is not far. On race days, the area around Nakayama is thick with cars and buses, so check the calendar. Funabashi's name means boat bridge, a reminder that the city began as a landing place for ships on the old Edo coastal route.

The bay itself has a story. Until the 1960s, the shallow waters off Funabashi were a major fishing ground, and the Sanbanze tidal flat, a protected wetland south of the city, is still a vital stopover for migrating birds. Funabashi was famous for its seaweed and clams, and a few old fishing families remain. The city also has a ski dome and a large shopping centre, a sign of how much the area has changed.

Fuel and food are plentiful, with stations on the main roads and a huge variety of restaurants. The city's fresh seafood and, nearby, the peanut products of Chiba are typical local items, and a bowl of ramen is always easy to find. The JR and Tobu lines, and the subway, connect the city to Tokyo.

If you have time, take the road to the Sanbanze wetland and watch the birds at dusk. The flat light on the water is very calm.
t.fukushima@37.8,140.5:
Fukushima is a city of fruit. Its basin, ringed by mountains, produces peaches, pears, apples and grapes, and in spring the slopes are pink and white with blossom. It is the start and the end of the Bandai-Azuma Skyline ride, and the first view of the mountains is a promise.

The Bandai-Azuma Skyline is a toll road that climbs from Tsuchiyu hot spring up to a high plateau at around sixteen hundred metres, where the road runs across a volcanic landscape of bare rock, steam vents and alpine plants. The bends are wide and open, the surface is excellent, and the views on a clear day are extensive. The road is closed in winter, usually from late November until April, and fog and wind can be dramatic at the top. Autumn colours, in October, are the best time to ride. Traffic is moderate, though weekends in the leaf season are busy.

Fukushima has a rich culture. The old castle town has a quiet centre with a museum, and Iizaka hot spring, to the north, has public baths where you can bathe in the soft, hot water. The area is also known for its sake and its peaches, which are sold in summer at roadside stalls. The region suffered in 2011 from the earthquake and nuclear accident, and the recovery has been long, but the countryside is open and welcoming. Mount Shinobu, a small hill in the city, has a park and a sweeping view.

Fuel and food are no problem in Fukushima, which has stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and it is wise to fill up before heading into the mountains, where stations are few. Local dishes include ramen, with a simple soy broth, and ika ninjin, a dish of squid and carrot.

Linger at the station if you arrive by train, and look at the Azuma range. The shape of the mountains explains the road ahead.
t.modernist kaunas architecture of optimis:
For twenty years between the wars, Kaunas was the capital of Lithuania in everything but name. Vilnius had been seized by Poland in 1920, so the government settled on this river city as a temporary seat, and the temporary arrangement lasted until 1939. In those two decades the town doubled in size and filled with new ministries, schools, banks, cinemas and apartment blocks in the clean, white, rounded style of the time. UNESCO listed the best of it in 2023 as the Architecture of Optimism, and the name fits: these are buildings designed by people who believed that a small country could start again.

The best way to see it is to walk or ride slowly along Laisvės alėja, the long pedestrian boulevard through the centre, then drift north and east through the neighbourhoods around it. The Central Post Office, with its rational lines and tall clock, is one stop; the Vytautas the Great War Museum, with a garden and a bell tower, is another. On the hill of Žaliakalnis, a funicular climbs through quiet villa streets to the huge Christ's Resurrection Church, a pale, boxy giant begun in the 1930s as a national thanksgiving and used for decades as a radio factory under the Soviets. From the roof terrace you see the whole sprawl of the town spread across the confluence of the Nemunas and Neris.

For a rider, Kaunas is a normal city with some old-fashioned habits. The centre has tram-less streets, patchy cobbles in the older quarter, and plenty of one-way systems. Drivers can be impatient, and the long Soviet-era avenues invite speed, so watch for cameras. The road from Vilnius and Trakai on the A1 motorway is fast and easy, and the old Kaunas lagoon, a reservoir made in 1959, gives a pleasant detour toward the baroque monastery at Pažaislis, whose white and ochre domes reflect in the water.

With nearly four hundred thousand people, fuel, food and repairs are everywhere. Local cafés in the old modernist buildings are an attraction in themselves, and a cup of coffee in one makes a good rest.

Check the weather: Lithuanian spring and autumn can turn wet quickly, and wet cobbles are not friendly to a loaded bike.
t.warsaw@52.2,21.0:
Warsaw is a city that was erased and then rebuilt, and the second part is what makes it extraordinary. In August 1944 the Polish Home Army rose against the German occupiers, and after two months of fighting the Germans, on Hitler's orders, systematically destroyed most of the city, leaving it a field of rubble. The Old Town was reconstructed after the war, brick by brick, using old paintings, notably those of the eighteenth-century artist Bernardo Bellotto, and documents saved by the city's architects. UNESCO listed the result in 1980 as a remarkable act of cultural will.

With about one and three quarter million people, Warsaw today is a bustling capital of glass towers and trams, with the great Vistula River flowing through the middle. The Palace of Culture and Science, a Stalinist skyscraper given by the Soviet Union in the 1950s, is the city's most debated landmark, and many people joke that the best view of Warsaw is from the top, since it is the only place that you cannot see it. Elsewhere, there are green parks like Łazienki, with its palace on the water and peacocks, and the Chopin Museum, since the composer grew up here. Marie Curie was born in the city as well.

The food is good and unpretentious, with dumplings, soups, grilled sausages and a vigorous coffee scene. The modern city has restaurants of every type, and the Praga district, across the river, has become a lively area of galleries and bars.

As the start of a long day trip to the south-east, Warsaw demands patience. The traffic is heavy, the ring roads congested at rush hour, and the trams, cobbles and tramlines in the old streets can be slippery when wet. Once out on the expressways, the riding is fast and flat, through farmland, and the surfaces are generally excellent. Speed cameras are widespread and Polish police are strict, so keep to the limits.

Fuel and services are everywhere, and you should fill up before leaving, since you will have a long distance to cover. Park the bike in a secure place, and use the efficient public transport to see the old town.

Leave early, ideally before seven, and you will clear the suburbs before the traffic builds. The reward is a long day in the open countryside.
t.krzemionki prehistoric striped flint min:
Five thousand years ago, people in these low wooded hills in the Świętokrzyskie region were digging down into the ground for a stone that looked like nothing else. Striped flint, with its bands of grey, brown and cream, is a rarity, and it was prized for making polished axes that were traded across a large part of central Europe. The mines at Krzemionki, along with sites at Borownia, Korycizna and Wierzbica, make up one of the most extensive prehistoric mining landscapes known, and UNESCO listed the group in 2019.

The mining began in the late Neolithic and continued for a long time, perhaps from around 3900 BC to about 1600 BC, with miners sinking shafts into the limestone and following the seam of flint through underground galleries. The tools were simple, made of antler, stone and wood, and the miners worked in near darkness, hauling out the nodules in baskets. They left behind thousands of pits and tunnels, and the surface above is dotted with hollows, now covered in oak and pine forest. The flint travelled hundreds of kilometres as axe heads, a symbol of status and skill, and you can find them in museums from the Baltic to the Carpathians.

The area is gentle, with low sandy hills, mixed forest, farmland and small villages, and it smells of resin on warm days. It is a quiet region, and a fine place for a slow picnic. The nature around the site is rich, with woodpeckers, orchids in spring and bats that winter underground.

The ride in from the capital is mostly fast, flat road through the Mazovian plain, then through gentler country as you approach the hills. Surfaces are generally good, but the last kilometres are on small roads, sometimes narrow, with farm vehicles, cyclists and the occasional horse cart. Summer thunderstorms are common, and the roads can be slick after rain. Take care at level crossings and on blind bends.

For fuel, Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about nine kilometres away, is the larger town, with stations, supermarkets and cafes, and the villages nearby, such as Bałtów and Ćmielów, have little. Fill up there and bring water.

The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the forest is green or golden and the heat is mild. Allow time to walk, as the interest lies in the slow understanding of what the land holds.
t.krzemionki opatowskie mining field@51.0,:
This is the place where you can actually go down. The Krzemionki Opatowskie mining field has an underground tourist route of about half a kilometre, through a network of old galleries, chambers and narrow passages cut by Neolithic miners and then protected for visitors. The temperature below the ground stays cool all year, so bring a sweater even in August, and the air has the damp, mineral smell of old stone. A guide leads you through, with a light that picks out the striped flint in the walls, and the pits where miners once worked by the light of fires.

It is a strange feeling to stand in a space dug five thousand years ago with tools of antler and stone. The miners, who lived in settlements in the surrounding hills, dug shafts up to about nine metres deep and then tunnelled outwards along the flint-bearing layer, leaving pillars of rock to hold up the roof. In some chambers you can see the marks of their picks. The scale of the operation, with thousands of shafts across the field, suggests an organised community, perhaps with specialised workers and traders, which surprises people who imagine prehistoric Europe as a land of scattered hunters.

A small museum and reconstructed Neolithic settlement near the entrance help explain the context, and the forest around is a nature reserve, with oaks, pines and a rich ground cover of flowers in spring. The access is by a short forest path from the car park, and the tour takes about an hour, so check the opening times and book ahead in busy periods, since numbers underground are limited.

Riding here is quiet and pleasant. The roads through the Świętokrzyskie hills are gentle, with moderate bends and good tarmac for the most part, and the traffic is light outside the summer weekends. Watch for deer at dusk and for tractors on narrow roads. Spring and autumn rains can leave leaves and mud on the verges.

Fuel is a matter of planning. Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about nine kilometres away, has several stations, shops and restaurants, while the nearby villages offer little, and Ćmielów, with its famous porcelain factory, is a good stop for a coffee. Bring a layer for the cold underground, and a waterproof for the walk.

Arrive early, before the tour groups, and you will have the galleries almost to yourself.
t.borownia mining field@50.9,21.6:
Borownia is the quiet cousin among the flint mining fields, and that is part of its charm. Where Krzemionki has a visitor centre and a guided underground route, Borownia is a forested landscape of low hills, in which the traces of Neolithic mining appear as a scatter of shallow hollows on the forest floor. It is one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of 2019, and its value lies in showing how widely the mining spread across the district, rather than in a single dramatic display.

The area is part of the foothills of the Świętokrzyskie Mountains, a region of old rounded ridges, rich in ancient rocks, some of the oldest in Poland. The forests are mostly pine and oak, with birch on the sandy ground, and in late summer the air is full of the smell of resin and warm needles. Mushroom pickers walk the woods in autumn, and you may see them at the roadside with baskets of boletes. Deer, foxes and wild boar live in the woods, and the birdsong in spring is loud.

Nearby, the small town of Ćmielów, about five kilometres away, has been making porcelain since the late eighteenth century, and its factory and museum are well worth a visit. Ożarów, a little farther, is known for cement. Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, the larger town, was a centre of steel making for generations, and some of the old industrial buildings are still standing.

Riding in the area is gentle and unhurried, along small roads through forest and fields, with easy bends and few vehicles. The surface varies, from fine tarmac to patched and potholed stretches, and gravel can lie at the corners, especially after farm traffic. In summer, thunderstorms build in the afternoon and can be violent. It is not a place for speed, but for the pleasure of low hills and long shadows.

For fuel, the best choice is Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about thirteen kilometres away, which has stations, supermarkets and a good selection of cafes. Smaller places nearby may have a shop but not a pump. Bring water, since walking in the forest in summer is thirsty work.

The best time to see the landscape is in the early morning, when the mist hangs among the trees. Borownia rewards those who like to look at the ground and imagine what lies beneath.
t.bialystok@53.1,23.2:
Białystok is the capital of Podlasie, the north-eastern corner of Poland, and a city with a surprisingly cosmopolitan past. Around 290,000 people live here now, but the historical mix was far richer, with Poles, Jews, Belarusians, Lithuanians, Tatars and Russians all contributing to the character of the town. In the nineteenth century it grew into a textile centre, and before the Second World War, Jews made up a majority of its population, a history that ended in the Holocaust and is remembered in several memorials around the city.

One native son changed the world in a quiet way. Ludwik Zamenhof, born here in 1859, created Esperanto, a language designed to let people of different nationalities speak to each other on equal terms, partly in response to the quarrels of languages he heard in his childhood streets. A small museum and a monument keep his memory alive, and the city still hosts Esperanto events.

The most striking building is the Branicki Palace, a baroque residence of the eighteenth century with formal gardens, often called the Versailles of Podlasie. Its white façade, gilded gates and statues are an unexpected luxury on the plains. Nearby, the town hall, cathedral and a mix of Orthodox, Catholic and Lutheran churches show the layered history of the region. Food here is the food of the borderlands, with potato dumplings, a cold beetroot soup in summer and sękacz, a tall spit cake with a rippled surface.

For a rider, Białystok is a base for exploring the forests and wetlands of the east. The road to Białowieża, about eighty kilometres to the south-east, runs through farmland and then forest, with long straights and gentle bends, and traffic is moderate. Watch for tractors, horse carts and deer, and take care in fog, which can settle on the plains in autumn and winter. Cobbles and tram tracks in the older streets can be slippery.

Fuel and services are everywhere in the city, and you should fill up before heading out, since the villages on the way have fewer stations. Wasilków, a smaller town a few kilometres away, has more options than you would expect.

Leave in the morning, and give yourself time to stop in the villages with their brightly painted wooden houses.
t.bialowieza forest@52.7,23.9:
There is nowhere else in lowland Europe quite like Białowieża. The forest straddles the border between Poland and Belarus, and it is the last large remnant of the primeval woodland that once covered the plains of the continent. Some of its trees are centuries old, towering oaks, limes, hornbeams and spruces, and the ground is littered with fallen trunks, which are left to rot as they would be in nature, and which feed an astonishing variety of fungi, beetles and birds. UNESCO listed it in 1979 and later extended the listing to include the Belarusian side.

The star is the European bison, the żubr, a heavy, shaggy animal that was hunted to extinction in the wild in the early twentieth century. A few animals survived in zoos, and breeding programmes returned them to this forest in the 1950s, so that today several hundred roam the Polish side. They are shy, and you are more likely to meet one by chance on a forest path than on a planned walk, but a show reserve near the village keeps some animals in large enclosures. Wolves, lynx, elk and a long list of woodpeckers, including the white-backed, also live here.

The village of Białowieża, with fewer than three thousand people, has wooden houses with carved trims, a small museum, a palace park and a spirit of calm. Part of the forest is a national park, which can be entered only on foot with a licensed guide, and the rest is accessible on marked trails and bicycle routes. A lime-lined road leads in from the east, and the air is damp and cool beneath the trees.

For motorcyclists the roads are quiet, with gentle bends and long straights through forest, and traffic is light, though tourist buses can be slow in summer. Watch for animals at dusk, especially deer and wild boar, and for ruts in the surface after winter frosts. Be aware that the area near the Belarusian border has been subject to restrictions in recent years, so check current rules before you set out.

Fuel is not available in the forest itself, and the nearest town with services is Hajnówka, about twenty-one kilometres away. Fill up there, and bring food and water.

Come in late May or early autumn, when the light is soft and the forest is full of birdsong.
t.bia owieza forest@52.7,24.0:
Here the forest gets closer to the border, and the history in the air gets heavier. For centuries this was a royal hunting ground, preserved by Polish kings and Lithuanian grand dukes and later by the Russian tsars, who made it one of the best-protected game reserves in Europe, and it was this protection that kept the forest alive.

One famous event took place on the Belarusian side. In December 1991, in a hunting lodge in the forest, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the agreement that dissolved the Soviet Union. A forest that had survived tsars and wars had a part in the end of an empire. On the Polish side, the traces of the border are more mundane but also visible, with fences, patrol vehicles and the discreet infrastructure of a frontier that has become tense in recent years.

The population here is an unusual mix. Many villagers belong to the Orthodox Church and speak a local dialect with Belarusian roots, and the wooden village churches, with onion domes and blue and white painting, stand beside meadows. Hajnówka, the main town of the district, has a strong Orthodox character and an Orthodox church of striking modern design. The food is simple and rich, with potato pancakes, mushrooms and dairy.

Riding on the minor roads here is a gentle pleasure, with straight stretches through the trees, occasional bends and little traffic. The surface can be rough in places, and the shaded roads stay damp and mossy in the mornings. Animals are a hazard, particularly at dusk, and the forest swallows mobile phone signals in places. Because of the border, there may be checkpoints and restricted zones, so carry identification and follow instructions.

Fuel can be found in Hajnówka, around twenty-seven kilometres from this point, and you should fill up there. Białowieża village has shops and cafes, but no reliable fuel.

Autumn is a splendid season, with golden leaves and rutting bison, though the mist can be thick. Summer brings mosquitoes, so keep covered when you stop.
t.lake itasca@47.2,-95.2:
You can walk across the Mississippi here without getting your knees wet. At the north end of Lake Itasca, in a state park of pine forest and small lakes in north-western Minnesota, the river starts as a gentle outflow about twenty feet wide over a line of stepping stones, and from this spot it begins a journey of roughly 2,340 miles to the Gulf of Mexico. Visitors take the obligatory photograph on the rocks, and some cannot resist the wade, but the trickle looks nothing like the vast brown river that passes New Orleans.

The name has a story. In 1832 the explorer Henry Schoolcraft, guided by an Ojibwe man called Ozawindib, reached this lake, which he believed to be the source, and coined its name from the Latin words veritas caput, meaning true head. Native peoples had known the area long before, and the Ojibwe name for the river, Misi-ziibi, simply means great river. Itasca became Minnesota's first state park in 1891, protecting some of the last stands of old red and white pine in the region, and the forest is a good reason to linger. Walk a trail in the early morning and you may hear loons calling over the water.

The Great River Road starts here, marked by green signs with a pilot's wheel, and it follows the Mississippi downstream through five states or more. The first miles are gentle and rural, on two-lane roads through lakes, pine, farmland and small towns, with curves that are more rolling than technical. The surface is generally good, deer are the main danger at dusk, and mosquitoes and biting flies can be fierce in early summer. Because of that, many riders prefer September, when the leaves turn gold and the air is crisp.

Fuel is not available in the park itself, and the nearest larger town is Bemidji, about 35 kilometres away, famous for its statues of Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox. Park Rapids and Bagley are smaller options. A state park vehicle permit is required to enter, and the summer season is busy on weekends. Bring a jacket, since nights are cool even in July.
t.medina@29.8,-99.2:
Medina is apple country, which is not what most people expect of Texas. Up here in the western Hill Country, the elevation and cooler nights let orchards thrive, and the little town on the Medina River has made itself the Apple Capital of Texas, with roadside stands selling pies, cider and fresh fruit from late summer into fall. The shops have a rustic, Western look, with porches, hitching rails and a feeling of being a long way from anywhere.

The surrounding land is the Edwards Plateau, a limestone upland carved into hills and valleys by rivers, with scrubby live oak and Ashe juniper, locally called cedar, covering the slopes. Clear, spring-fed rivers run through narrow canyons, and the Medina River, a few miles away, is one of the prettiest. Bandera, a short ride east, calls itself the Cowboy Capital of the World, with dance halls and rodeos, and Kerrville to the north is a larger town with a long river park and a folk music festival in spring.

For riders, Medina is the gateway to the roads that locals call the Twisted Sisters. These are three Ranch Roads, 335, 336 and 337, that run west toward Leakey and Camp Wood, climbing and diving through the canyon country in a string of tight curves and steep gradients. They are some of the most famous motorcycle roads in the Southwest, and on weekends the area is full of riders. The surface is mostly good, though cattle guards and low-water crossings call for care, and cattle and deer sometimes stand on the road. Gravel on the corners is common, and the shoulders are narrow.

Medina has fuel, a store or two and a few places to eat, but it is wise to fill up here, since the roads west have long gaps between stations. Kerrville and Bandera have larger supermarkets. The best seasons are spring, when the wildflowers, especially bluebonnets, carpet the roadsides, and autumn, when the heat has broken. Summer afternoons are hot, often well over thirty-five degrees Celsius, and sudden thunderstorms can flood the low crossings. Carry water, and start early.
t.gizycko@54.0,21.8:
Giżycko lies on a narrow strip of land between two big lakes, Niegocin and Kisajno, in the middle of the Masurian Lake District, and the setting is the whole story. The region, Mazury, has some two thousand lakes, linked by canals and rivers, scattered among forests and fields in the north-east of Poland, and Giżycko is its sailing capital, with a harbor full of yachts, a pier and a lakeside promenade where families eat ice cream in summer.

The town's German name was Lötzen, and for centuries this was part of East Prussia. The Prussians built a star-shaped fortress here in the mid-nineteenth century, the Boyen Fortress, named for a Prussian general, with thick brick walls and bastions that now form a park. After 1945 the area became Polish, and the town was renamed after Gustaw Gizewiusz, a Lutheran pastor who championed Masurian culture. A rotating bridge over the canal, still turned by hand, is a curious attraction. The Wolf's Lair, Hitler's wartime headquarters, lies in the forest near Kętrzyn, about forty kilometers away, where the 1944 bomb plot against him took place.

For riding, the lakes area is flat to gently rolling, with straight roads through forests of pine and birch, tree-lined avenues of old oaks and lindens, and glimpses of water between the trees. National roads 59 and 63 run through the area, with moderate traffic, and the side roads are quieter. It is a peaceful, restful kind of riding, and the storks that nest on poles and chimneys in the villages add to the charm. Tractors and horse carts are common, and in Poland you must use dipped headlights at all times.

Giżycko has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and many guesthouses, and it is a good base for exploring. The local cuisine features freshwater fish, smoked eel, pierogi and mushroom dishes. The best months are June to September, with warm days and long light, though July and August bring crowds. Spring and autumn are quieter, and winter freezes the lakes, with ice sailing on the Masurian waters. Deer and wild boar cross the roads at dusk, so slow down in forested stretches.
t.olsztyn@53.8,20.5:
Olsztyn is the capital of Warmia and Masuria, a region of forests and lakes in northern Poland that has the nickname of the land of a thousand lakes, although the real count is higher. The town lies on the river Łyna, with water on almost every side. Its medieval brick castle, built by the cathedral chapter of Warmia in the fourteenth century, looks over the old town, and the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus lived in it for several years in the early sixteenth century as administrator of the chapter's estates. A table of the equinoxes that he drew on a cloister wall can still be seen.

The old town is compact, with brick gabled houses, a high gate and a market square that comes alive in summer with outdoor tables. The city later became a university town, and student energy fills the cafes. An unusual note is the chapel of the Jewish cemetery, designed by the architect Erich Mendelsohn, who was born in the city.

For riders, the countryside around Olsztyn is the attraction. Tree-lined avenues of old lime and maple, some planted centuries ago, arch over the tarmac, and the roads wind gently past lakes, forests and fields. The tarmac is generally good, though minor roads may have patches. The riding is more about the rhythm and the light than about tight bends. Cranes, storks and herons are common, and in early autumn the lakes can be wrapped in mist at dawn.

Further east, the Great Masurian Lakes around Mikołajki offer sailing and quiet roads, but they fill with holidaymakers in July and August. Choose May, June or September for emptier roads. Be careful at dusk, when deer cross, and keep to the speed limits, since Polish police use roadside cameras and patrol cars.

Olsztyn has plenty of stations and supermarkets. Try pierogi, smoked fish from the lakes and a plate of potato dumplings with mushroom sauce.
t.tsuchiyu pass@37.7,140.2:
Tsuchiyu Pass is a mountain crossing at about 1,240 metres in the Azuma range of Fukushima, and it is the doorway to one of the great volcanic roads of northern Japan. Below it, on the Fukushima side, is Tsuchiyu Onsen, a small hot spring village in a steep, wooded gorge, where the water is acid, milky and slightly sulphurous, and the local craft is the making of kokeshi, the slim wooden dolls with round heads that are a symbol of the Tohoku region. Above the pass, the Bandai-Azuma Skyline climbs onto a lava plateau of bare rock, steaming vents and views that stretch across the whole prefecture.

The Skyline is a toll road, about twenty-eight kilometres long, linking Tsuchiyu with the Takayu area, and it is the main reason motorcyclists come. It rises out of cedar and beech forest to the open slopes of the volcanic peaks, with a series of broad, flowing bends and long views across the Inawashiro basin and the lake. The surface is excellent, the gradient is moderate and the traffic is light, especially on weekdays. Near the highest section, the barren slopes of Mount Issaikyo, with their yellow and white sulphur deposits and steaming fumaroles, look more like another planet than northern Japan. Gas from the vents can be strong in places, and visitors with respiratory problems should take care.

The road is closed in winter, usually from late autumn to April or May, when snow and ice make it impassable, and in spring the walls of snow at the roadside can be several metres high. Autumn colour here in October is famous, and the mountain flanks turn red, orange and yellow, drawing crowds on weekends. Fog and sudden rain are common, and the temperature at the top can be much lower than in the valley, so a warm layer and a waterproof are a good idea.

Tsuchiyu Onsen has public baths, small inns and noodle shops, and a hot spring soak after a long ride is one of the real pleasures of Japan. There are rest areas along the Skyline with simple food. For fuel, Inawashiro, about sixteen kilometres away, and Fukushima city, on the other side of the range, have the nearest stations, so fill before climbing, as there is none on the toll road itself.

The mountains here are part of the Bandai-Asahi National Park, and the sulphurous air and the soft light on the grass give the area a peculiarly northern Japanese character, quiet and a little austere.
t.kokelv@70.6,24.7:
Kokelv is a hamlet on the shore of the Kvalsund, in Finnmark, and it is where the road to Havøysund begins its journey north to the Barents Sea. At nearly seventy-one degrees north, this is deep in the Arctic, and the landscape is open and treeless, with low hills, rocky shores and a sky that dominates everything. Hammerfest, the northernmost town in the world of any size, is about thirty-six kilometres away, and Rypefjord, the smaller port, is nearly the same distance, so fuel and supplies come from there. Kokelv has only a few buildings and a small harbour.

Finnmark is the home of the Sami, the indigenous people of northern Scandinavia, and reindeer herding is still a living tradition. In spring and summer, herds move toward the coast to graze, and in autumn they return inland, and on the roads you will often see reindeer standing in the verge or crossing without hurry. Slow down and give them room, because collisions are common. The Sami language is heard here, and place names appear in both Norwegian and Sami on signs.

The road north follows the coast and crosses a landscape of bare rock, bogs and low scrub. It is narrow and mostly well surfaced, with long straight sections and occasional bends. Wind is a major factor: in Finnmark, storms can be strong and cold, and gusts can push a bike across the lane. Weather changes quickly, and fog can roll in from the sea. In winter, the road can close, and in the shoulder seasons, ice is possible in the early morning. Summer, from June to August, is the main season, with the midnight sun shining from mid-May to late July.

Be self-sufficient. There are very few services between Kokelv and Havøysund, and the distances feel greater than they look on a map. Fill the tank in Hammerfest, carry water and a warm layer, and check the opening hours of any ferry or tunnel. The air here is clean and cold, with a smell of salt and peat, and the open view can be strangely calming. At night in summer, the sun skims the horizon, and the colours of the sea turn soft pink and gold.
t.snefjord@70.8,24.6:
Snefjord is a small settlement on a fjord of the same name in the far north of Finnmark, in a landscape that has more sky than land. At seventy degrees north, the trees have given up, and what is left is tundra, low birch scrub in the hollows, bare rock, lakes and long hills the colour of old rope. The road to Havøysund, the fishing village at the end of the peninsula, crosses this country and drops down to the fjords at intervals, and Snefjord is one of those places where you suddenly find water, boats and a handful of houses at the foot of the hills.

For a rider, the road is a long, quiet, rolling one. The surface is generally good, the bends are gentle, and there is little traffic apart from the occasional truck, a fisherman's pickup and, in summer, campervans. Distances are large and the villages are far apart. The wind is the main hazard, as there is nothing to stop it, and on the high stretches gusts can be strong. Snow can come early in the autumn and stay late in the spring, and in winter the road is often closed or convoy-led, so check conditions before you set out.

This is Sami country, and reindeer herding is part of life here, as it has been for centuries. In summer the herds move to the coast to graze and escape the insects, and you may find them on the road. They have no sense of traffic, and a rider should slow right down. From mid-May to late July the sun does not set, and the light has a golden, low-angled quality that makes everything look closer.

Fuel is a serious matter. Hammerfest, the nearest town of any size, is a long way off, and Havøysund has a pump but it is at the end of the road. Fill up before you set out and carry a little extra if you can. Food and coffee are rare on the road itself, so bring a flask and a sandwich. Mobile signal fades in the fjords, and there is no help for many kilometres, so tell someone your plan. The reward is silence, space and the strange northern light.
t.lillefjord@70.9,24.7:
Lillefjord is a tiny village along the road to Havøysund, its houses lined up along a small fjord on the coast of Finnmark, with the Barents Sea out beyond. The name means little fjord, and it fits. The landscape around it is stark: bare hills, smooth rock scoured by ice, and a few fishing boats on the water. People have fished here for as long as anyone can say, and the village has a quiet, self-contained air, a place that does what it does and does not need to be noticed.

What matters to a rider in this part of Norway is the road and the weather. The route to Havøysund runs a long way through the treeless north, and reindeer are the most likely cause of delay, so keep an eye out and slow right down when you see them, because they will walk across the road without warning. The surface is good, and the corners are long and unhurried. There is little traffic, and when there is, it is polite. Winter driving can be harsh, with ice, snow and darkness, and the road can close in storms, so check before you commit to the trip.

From the middle of May until late July the sun does not set, and you can ride in full daylight at midnight, which feels odd and wonderful. In autumn and winter, the northern lights dance over the village on clear nights, green and sometimes red, and the quiet is complete. The best times for riding are June and August, when the days are long and the temperature is up to ten or fifteen degrees, though wind and rain are possible at any time. Pack warm layers, rain gear and gloves, and bring more than you think you need.

The nearest pumps are at Havøysund, at the end of the road, and at Hammerfest, which is much larger and has shops, a hospital and a proper choice of food. Make sure you leave Hammerfest with a full tank and a reserve in the pannier. If you are looking for a place to eat on the way, plan ahead, as little is open outside the summer season. A picnic by the fjord, with a view of fishing boats and the evening light, is a very good meal.
t.havoysund@71.0,24.7:
Havøysund is a fishing village on an island at the very north of Norway, at about seventy-one degrees north, and the road that leads to it is one of the northernmost in Europe. About a thousand people live here, in colourful wooden houses around a busy harbour, and the settlement exists for fish: cod, haddock and king crab, which arrived in the Barents Sea after being introduced by the Soviet Union and is now a valuable catch. The village was burned to the ground in 1944 when German forces retreated, as the whole of Finnmark was, and it was rebuilt after the war in a plain, practical style.

A bridge connects the island to the mainland, and the final stretch of road runs along the coast, past bare hills and rocky bays. The sea here is the Barents, cold and rich, and in summer, the sun stays in the sky around the clock. You may see sea eagles, eider ducks and, in the right season, whales offshore. The road is quiet and well maintained, though exposed to the wind, which can be fierce, particularly in autumn and winter. In summer, temperatures are cool and rain is frequent, so carry waterproofs.

Not far off, a wind farm stands on the hills near the village, one of the more curious sights in the Arctic. There is also a small sea-bird colony, and the headland near the village, with its lighthouse, is a good place to watch the waves. A coastal walk leads to a viewpoint, and there is a museum of local history. Visitors come mainly for the remote feel and the midnight sun.

Fuel and food are available in the village, but opening hours are limited, and it is wise to fill up before you set out. Local restaurants serve fresh seafood, including king crab, which is delicious and expensive. Accommodation is limited, so book ahead in summer. After a long ride across the empty north, it feels like arriving at the edge of the world, and the cold light on the water is an apt farewell.
t.zhovkva tserkva of the holy trinity@50.1:
Zhovkva was designed as an ideal Renaissance town. In the late sixteenth century, Stanisław Żółkiewski, a Polish nobleman and military commander, founded it north of Lviv with a castle, a market square, churches and fortifications laid out according to the principles of the time. Later, the town was a favourite residence of King Jan III Sobieski, who defeated the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683. The Tserkva of the Holy Trinity, a wooden church built in 1720, stands on the edge of the town, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, inscribed in 2013.

The church is made of wood, with three domes in the Ukrainian tradition, and inside, an iconostasis of carved and gilded wood with painted icons, made by local craftsmen. The wooden churches of the region show the skill of carpenters who built them without nails, using techniques passed down for generations.

Zhovkva has a castle, a Renaissance market square with arcades, a Catholic collegiate church, a Basilian monastery, and a fortified synagogue from the seventeenth century, a reminder of the large Jewish community that lived here before the Holocaust. The town has fuel, shops and restaurants.

A practical word: Ukraine is at war, under martial law, and many governments advise against all travel there. Even in the west, air raid alerts are frequent, curfews apply, and rules can change quickly, so check official advice, your insurance and entry requirements before considering a visit. In peacetime, the roads around Lviv are generally good, with rolling hills, forests and villages, and Lviv itself, a UNESCO-listed city of churches, coffee houses and cobbled streets, is one of the most beautiful in Eastern Europe. The Polish border is close, and Polish wooden churches, such as the one at Chotyniec, can be visited on the other side.
t.salt mine in bochnia@50.0,20.4:
People were mining salt at Bochnia by the middle of the thirteenth century, which makes it the oldest salt mine in Poland and one of the oldest in Europe still open to visitors. For centuries the salt from here and from Wieliczka, about twenty-five kilometres to the west, filled the coffers of the Polish kings; at times it accounted for a remarkable share of the royal income. Together the two mines and the royal castle at Wieliczka form a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Going down is the experience. A lift drops you deep underground into a world of tunnels, chambers and chapels carved out of grey salt, with wooden supports, old winches and machinery that tell the story of hard, dangerous work over seven centuries. Part of the tour is by underground railway, and there is a long wooden slide that visitors of all ages seem to enjoy far more than expected. The largest chamber, the Ważyn, has been used as a sports hall and a sanatorium, because the cool, salty air is believed to help breathing problems, and you can even spend the night down there.

Bochnia itself is a pleasant market town of around thirty thousand people, east of Kraków, with a square, a large Gothic basilica and the mine's headframe rising over the rooftops. The riding nearby is mostly flat to rolling, with busy main roads and the A4 motorway, which has tolls on some sections. Head south and things get much more interesting: the Beskid foothills begin within half an hour, with winding roads through wooded hills, wooden churches and small resort towns on the way towards the Tatra mountains.

Fuel, food and accommodation are easy to find in town. Bring a warm layer for the mine, where the temperature stays cool all year, and good shoes for the stairs and uneven floors. Polish home cooking is the perfect fuel for an underground adventure: pierogi with potato and cheese, żurek sour rye soup served in a bread bowl, or a hearty bowl of bigos, hunter's stew of cabbage and meat, washed down with compote or a cold local beer once the riding is done.
t.kernave archaeological site@54.9,24.9:
Five steep, grassy mounds rise above a bend in the Neris river about forty kilometres north-west of Vilnius, and from the top of them you look out over meadows, woods and water much as the medieval inhabitants did. This is Kernavė, the first capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and its hillforts and the remains of the town below make up a World Heritage site that covers ten thousand years of human settlement.

People camped here at the end of the Ice Age, and the site was occupied almost continuously through the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age. By the thirteenth century, Kernavė was a thriving town of craftsmen and traders, with wooden castles on the hilltops, and it served as a seat of Lithuanian rulers. In 1390 it was burned by the Teutonic Knights, and the capital moved to Vilnius. The town was never rebuilt on the same scale, which is why so much remains buried in the ground, giving archaeologists a remarkable record of medieval life.

Riding to Kernavė is easy and pleasant. From Vilnius, the roads run through gently rolling countryside, past villages, lakes and forests, with smooth surfaces and light traffic. The final approach drops into the Neris valley, offering a fine view of the hillforts. Lithuania is mostly flat, so this is not a place for dramatic mountain roads, but the scenery is calm and green, especially in late spring and summer. Winters are cold and snowy, and roads can be icy.

The Neris valley is lush and peaceful, with meadows full of wildflowers, oak and pine woods, and birds such as storks, cranes and herons. In early summer, the site hosts a festival of experimental archaeology, where people in medieval costume demonstrate crafts, cooking and battles. The midsummer night celebrations, known as Joninės, are also celebrated here with bonfires and singing.

Kernavė has a small museum, a café and limited services. For fuel, Vievis, about thirteen kilometres away, and Širvintos are the closest towns, while Elektrėnai is a bit further but larger. Vilnius, with its baroque old town, is less than an hour away. Try cepelinai, the hearty potato dumplings, or kibinai, savoury pastries from the Karaim community in nearby Trakai.
t.radruz tserkva of saint paraskeva@50.2,2:
In the hills of south-eastern Poland, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, a small wooden church stands in a green yard by the village of Radruz, beneath tall trees. It is the tserkva of Saint Paraskeva, dating from the early sixteenth century, and it is one of the finest wooden churches in the Carpathian region, inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 with fifteen others in Poland and Ukraine. The nearest settlement is Horyniec-Zdroj, a spa village of two thousand seven hundred people three kilometres away, and the larger town of Rava-Ruska lies across the border in Ukraine.

Tserkva is the Ukrainian word for church, and these buildings were built by the Greek Catholic and Orthodox communities of the Boyko and Lemko peoples, with steep shingled roofs, three domed sections and, usually, a separate wooden belfry. Radruz is built of horizontal logs, with a low, dark interior full of old icons, and the walls and ceiling are covered with painted scenes. A carved iconostasis separates the nave from the sanctuary. The village was Ukrainian until after the Second World War, when its inhabitants were forcibly moved in the 1940s, in an operation named Vistula, and the church passed through a long period of neglect before being restored and made into a museum.

The surrounding country is Roztocze, a range of low, wooded hills that stretches from Poland into Ukraine, with beech and fir forests, small farms and meadows. The roads are narrow and quiet, with gentle bends and sudden dips, patched surfaces, and the occasional horse cart or tractor. Summer days are warm and green, and autumn colours are lovely, while winter brings snow and ice. Fog is common in the early morning. The border region has checkpoints, and there are restrictions near the frontier, so carry your passport and check the current situation, since the war in Ukraine affects travel in the area.

Horyniec-Zdroj has fuel, a few shops, a spa and several guesthouses. Larger towns such as Lubaczow and Cieszanow offer more choice. Local food is hearty, with pierogi, borscht, potato pancakes and sausage, and a glass of mead or fruit cordial is common. The church is open at set hours in season, so check before you go, and remember to dress respectfully and keep your voice low inside.
t.wieliczka and bochnia royal salt mines@5:
Under the town of Wieliczka, at the southern edge of the Krakow suburbs, lies a labyrinth of tunnels, chambers and lakes cut out of salt, nine levels deep, with the lowest more than three hundred metres below the surface. Salt has been mined here since the thirteenth century, and the mine, together with the one at Bochnia some twenty kilometres east, was one of the first sites placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, in 1978. Wieliczka has nearly nineteen thousand people, and the mine entrance is about a kilometre from the centre.

Salt was as valuable as gold in the Middle Ages, and royal salt revenues paid for much of the Polish crown's spending, which helped Krakow to grow rich. The miners worked in the dark with picks and horses, and over the centuries they carved chapels out of the rock salt, with altars, pulpits and statues, all of salt. The biggest, the Chapel of Saint Kinga, is an underground cathedral more than a hundred metres below the surface, with chandeliers of salt crystals and bas-reliefs, including a version of the Last Supper carved in the wall. Saint Kinga, a Hungarian princess who became a Polish duchess, is the patron of miners, and legend says she threw her ring into a Hungarian salt mine and it was found in Wieliczka. The air underground is about fourteen degrees all year and good for the lungs, and a small sanatorium exists in the depths.

The tourist route covers only a small part of the mine, about three kilometres, and starts with a long descent on wooden stairs, a few hundred steps, followed by a lift back to the surface. Tickets sell fast at weekends, so book ahead and allow about three hours.
