Wear comfortable shoes and a jacket, because the temperature is cool, and note that large bags may need to be left in the cloakroom.

For a rider, Wieliczka is a short hop from Krakow along busy roads, with heavy traffic at rush hour and congested streets near the entrance. The foothills of the Beskids to the south offer pleasant roads through villages and orchards, with the Tatra mountains visible in the distance on clear days. Fuel is on every main road, and the local cooking is generous, with pierogi, soup in bread bowls and sausages. Spring and autumn are lovely, summer is crowded, and winter is cold and grey.
t.transferdalen@70.0,23.5:
Alta is the biggest town in Finnmark, the northernmost county of Norway, and it lies at the head of a fjord far inside the Arctic Circle, on the same latitude as northern Alaska and the Siberian coast. East of town, the valley called Transferdalen cuts into the plateau, a place of birch and willow on its lower slopes and bare, rounded fell above, with a river in the bottom and Sámi names on the maps. The peak whose name appears on the ride titles, Luvdiidcohkka, is one of those Sámi names, and the Sámi, whose reindeer herds still move across this land, are the people who have known it longest.

The best-known thing in Alta is the rock art. Along the fjord at Hjemmeluft, thousands of carvings were made by hunter-gatherers between about 6000 and 2000 BC, showing reindeer, elk, boats, bears and people dancing, and UNESCO listed them in 1985. They were cut into the glaciated rock at what was then the seashore, and the land has risen since, so that they now lie above the water. The Alta Museum tells the story well, and there is a boardwalk that wanders past the panels in the open air. The town's other landmark is the Northern Lights Cathedral, a spiral of titanium opened in 2013.

Riding in Finnmark is something you should plan for. The E6 runs north to the Nordkapp and south along a huge empty coast, and the E45 heads inland toward Kautokeino across the high plain of the Finnmarksvidda, with a long, wide, lonely road. The road surface is generally good, but frost heaves and loose gravel can appear, and reindeer on the road are a real hazard, especially in summer and autumn. Never assume they will move. Weather turns quickly, and the wind off the fjord is cold even in July.

The midnight sun lasts from late May to late July, and the light on a summer night is golden and endless, though the mosquitoes in the birch woods are fierce. September and October bring auroras, and the autumn colours on the dwarf birch turn the fells red.

Fuel is in Alta, a town of about twelve thousand people, and it is wise to fill up and carry water and a snack before heading inland, where the next pump may be a long way off.
t.jododaira@37.7,140.3:
Jododaira, the name means Pure Land plain, and it is easy to see why. At about 1,600 metres on the Bandai-Azuma Skyline, the road crosses a high volcanic moor, a wide open space of grass, low shrubs and bare grey rock, with the steaming cone of Mount Issaikyo rising to one side. The ground smells faintly of sulphur, and wisps of white vapour drift from vents on the slopes. It feels like a different planet from the lowlands around Fukushima, and the name comes from Buddhist ideas of paradise.

The Skyline is a high road that links Fukushima city, via the hot spring village of Tsuchiyu, with the Bandai area to the south, and it crosses the shoulder of the Azuma volcanic range. It is one of the best mountain drives in the Tohoku region, with views over the whole of the Fukushima basin on one side and the wild country of the Azuma range on the other. Opening dates vary, but the road typically opens in late April, when the snow walls beside the road can still be several metres high, and closes in early November.

Behind the visitor centre, a boardwalk leads across the wetland, and a short trail climbs to the rim of Azuma-Kofuji, a small old crater where the ground is bare and cinder-red. The flora is alpine, with dwarf pines, cotton grass and in summer a scattering of wildflowers, and in autumn the slopes turn from green to copper and crimson in a few weeks, usually in early October at this height. Mount Issaikyo itself is active and can be closed to visitors when gas levels rise, so check before you walk.

The road has hairpins and long, smooth bends, with good tarmac and clear sightlines, and it is an easy but memorable ride. Be prepared for fog, wind and cold, since conditions can change in minutes. A small restaurant and shop near the visitor centre offers snacks and hot drinks, but opening hours are limited. Carry warm clothes, even in July, and be careful on the descent, where brakes work hard. Late September and early October bring the best colours and clear air.
t.arthur river@-41.0,144.7:
Arthur River is a fishing and holiday village at the mouth of a tannin-brown river on Tasmania's far north-west coast, and the people who live here describe the place as the end of the world with a straight face. A signboard on the rocky shore a few minutes away makes the claim official: the next land to the west is Argentina, about fifteen thousand kilometres across the Southern Ocean. The wind that arrives here has crossed nothing but water since South America, and it brings the long swells, the salt and a constant bright, wild light.

The river itself is the centrepiece. It runs dark as tea, stained by the buttongrass moorland and the rainforest of the Tarkine, the largest tract of temperate rainforest in Australia, and boat cruises take visitors upstream through myrtle and sassafras forest hung with moss. The Tarkine, called takayna in the language of the Aboriginal people of this coast, has a long history of human use, with middens along the shore and a deep cultural connection that goes back thousands of years. The beaches nearby are strewn with enormous bleached logs, driftwood carried down in floods and thrown back by the sea.

Riding here means a decision. The sealed road reaches the village from Smithton, and it is a pleasure, rolling through farmland, plantation and low forest. South of Arthur River the Western Explorer Road turns to gravel and crosses the wild interior toward Corinna, and that is a ride for a bike with proper tyres and a rider who is happy on loose surfaces. Even on the sealed section, the weather can be harsh, with sideways rain, strong gusts and a temperature that drops in minutes. Take a waterproof layer whatever the morning looks like.

The village is tiny and its services are small. There is a general store and a place to eat, but you should not assume that fuel is available on any given day, and the safe course is to fill the tank at Smithton, which is the nearest proper town, before you come out. Smithton has supermarkets, a bakery and a workshop, and it is the place to buy what you need.

The wildlife is part of the charm. Wallabies, pademelons and the occasional Tasmanian devil come out at dusk, and the road at night is a hazard, so plan to arrive before dark. In winter the village is often battered by storms, but the sea is spectacular. Spring and autumn offer the best compromise between light, calm and temperature.
t.kazimierz dolny@51.3,22.0:
Kazimierz Dolny looks like a town that has been preserved in amber, and the reason is quite simple: it grew rich, then it went quiet. In the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries it was a grain port on the Vistula, where merchants loaded wheat and rye onto barges bound for Gdańsk and the Baltic, and the money they made built the townhouses, with decorated gables and carved stone, that still surround the market square. When the river trade declined, the town stopped growing, and nobody rebuilt it. In the twentieth century painters found it, and artists have kept coming since.

The square is the centre of everything, with a well in the middle, cafes along the edges and shops selling pottery, paintings and the local speciality, a bread baked in the shape of a rooster. It is crowded on summer weekends, when coach parties and day trippers arrive from Warsaw, and magical on a weekday morning in May or October, when you can hear your own footsteps. Above the town, a ruined castle and a watchtower give a view over the river and the roofs, and the steep lanes that lead up to them are lined with old granaries.

The riding around it is distinctive. The land here is a loess upland, a soft yellow soil that rivers and rain have carved into deep, narrow gorges, and the roads follow them, sunk between high banks with tree roots hanging overhead. The surface is mostly good, the curves are gentle, and the real hazards are farm traffic, cyclists and the sheer number of tourists in the high season. On the other side of the Vistula, the land is flat and open, and you can cross by a small ferry to the castle ruins at Janowiec, which is a good reason to stay a bit longer.

Kazimierz is a small town, but it has fuel, cafes and restaurants, though prices rise and tables fill on weekends. Puławy, eleven kilometres away, is the larger town for anything more. Book accommodation ahead in the high season, and do not expect to park near the square. The best months are May and September, when the light is soft and the crowds are thin, and the willows along the river are in leaf.
t.wilkow@51.3,21.9:
Wilków is a village on the Vistula rather than a famous stop, and it earns its place on the ride through the country around it. The river here is wide, shallow and braided, running over sandbanks that appear and disappear with the season, and Poland has left it largely unregulated along this stretch, so it behaves much as it did centuries ago. White sandbars attract nesting terns and lapwings, willows and poplars crowd the banks, and in the evenings the whole valley is soft with mist and the sound of frogs.

Behind the river rises the edge of the Lublin Upland, with the loess gorges that are the district's signature. The roads here dip into them and climb out again, with surfaces that are generally good and bends that are gentle but constant. It is farming country, and in summer you pass orchards and fields of strawberries, cherries and apples, with stalls by the road selling the fruit in baskets. Fruit lorries and tractors are the main hazards in season, and the lanes are narrow enough that you cannot assume the other side is empty.

On the opposite bank, reached by the ferry that runs in the warmer months from nearby, stands the ruin of Janowiec Castle, a Renaissance residence that belonged to a succession of noble families and was left to decay after the wars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It is now a museum and a very atmospheric place to walk around, with views across the water. The ferry itself is half the fun: a short crossing, a few vehicles at a time, and a sense that the river is in charge. It does not run in the cold months, so check before you plan a loop.

Wilków has little in the way of services, so plan your stops. Kazimierz Dolny, eight kilometres away, is the obvious place for lunch, and Opole Lubelskie, fourteen kilometres off, is the nearest town of any size for fuel and shops, though Puławy is bigger still. Fill up before you head into the villages, and carry a bit of cash for farm stands, which do not always take cards. The late afternoon, with low sunlight on the river and the dust of the lanes glowing, is the time to be here.
t.mragowo@53.9,21.3:
Mrągowo is the biggest town in the heart of Masuria, a district in north-eastern Poland where glaciers left a maze of lakes, forests and low hills that Poles call the land of a thousand lakes. Until 1945 this was East Prussia, and the town was known as Sensburg; its Polish name and its present population came after the Second World War, when borders were redrawn and people moved. You can still find German-built brick churches and old villas in the older streets, and the layers of history are part of the town's character.

It sits on the shore of Lake Czos, with a pleasant promenade and a park, and it has become a holiday centre with an annual country music festival, the Piknik Country, which draws crowds from across Poland every summer. Outside the festival it is a calm, practical lake town of about twenty-two thousand people, with supermarkets, petrol stations and restaurants, and it makes a sensible base for exploring the surrounding area. The lakes are warm enough to swim in by July, and the forests hold mushroom pickers in autumn.

The roads of Masuria are gentle rather than dramatic, and that is their charm. They run through avenues of old lime and maple trees, past farms, lakes and small villages, with long straight sections broken by bends around the water. Surfaces are generally good, though patched in places, and the main hazards are tractors, slow-moving holiday traffic and, in summer, cyclists. Deer and wild boar cross at dusk, and storks nest on the village rooftops from spring to late summer. The old tree-lined roads can be dappled in sun and shade, which makes it hard to see the surface clearly, so ride a little slower than you might think.

Mrągowo has fuel, plenty of it, and it is the place to fill up before running the smaller villages and lake roads to the north and east. If you want a meal, the town has both quick cafes and more serious Polish kitchens, serving pierogi, grilled fish from the lakes and the heavy soups that suit a cold day. The best months are late spring and early autumn, when the weather is mild and the lakes are quiet.
t.miko ajki@53.8,21.6:
Mikołajki calls itself the pearl of Masuria, and for once the claim is not entirely marketing. The town is a small, well-kept place on a narrow strip of land between two lakes, Mikołajskie and Tałty, and a short canal away is Śniardwy, the largest lake in Poland. In summer the harbour is a forest of masts, as sailors from all over Poland and Germany move between the lakes, and the waterfront is full of people with ice cream and sunburn. A bronze statue of the King of the Whitefish, a creature from local legend, stands beside the water.

The history is mostly German, because until 1945 this was East Prussia, and the town was called Nikolaiken. The Masurian people who lived here were mostly Protestant and spoke a Polish dialect mixed with German, and a wave of resettlement after the war changed the population almost completely. The octagonal Protestant church, with its distinctive spire, is a landmark that you can see from the water. Near the town lies Lake Łuknajno, a nature reserve and part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, known for its large colony of mute swans, which gather in the hundreds.

On a motorcycle, the roads around Mikołajki are easy and scenic rather than exciting. They run along the lakes through forest and farmland, with tree-lined avenues and long, gentle bends, and the surface is mostly good. The real challenge is the volume of summer traffic, which on weekends can bring the road to a crawl, especially near the harbour and the ferry points. If you can, visit on a weekday, in the morning or in September, when the town is calm and the light is clear. A swim from one of the public beaches is a good break, though the water stays cold until well into June.

Mikołajki has fuel and a good range of restaurants, serving fish from the lakes, including smoked and fried varieties, and the usual Polish dishes. Mrągowo, nineteen kilometres away, is the larger town if you need more choice. Accommodation fills quickly in July and August, so book ahead if you are staying. Mosquitoes can be fierce around the water in the evening, and a light jacket is useful when the wind blows across the lake.
t.nowa s upia@50.9,21.1:
Nowa Słupia is a village that punches far above its weight in history, because it sits at the foot of the Holy Cross Mountains, the Góry Świętokrzyskie, among the oldest ranges in Europe. These hills are low, worn and wooded, rising to only a little over six hundred metres, but they have the dignity of age, with folds of rock dating back hundreds of millions of years. Beech and fir forest cover the slopes, and the road from the village climbs into them, with the smell of damp leaves and resin.

The village has a surprising claim: it was an ancient centre of iron-making. Archaeologists found thousands of smelting furnaces in the surrounding forest, dating back to the Roman period, when the local communities produced iron on a large scale, and each year in the summer the village hosts a festival in which people recreate the old smelting process in clay furnaces. There is a small museum of ancient metallurgy, and it is worth a short stop. The legend of the mountain, meanwhile, goes back further still, to pagan rituals on the summit before the arrival of Christianity.

Above the village stands the Benedictine abbey of Święty Krzyż, on Łysa Góra, the bald mountain, which holds what is said to be a relic of the True Cross. It has been a place of pilgrimage for centuries, and the buildings, though damaged by fire, war and neglect, still dominate the ridge. In the nineteenth century the monks were dispersed and the abbey was used as a prison, and in the Second World War it became a camp. Below the summit lies a field of huge quartzite boulders, the gołoborze, a rock river that formed in the last Ice Age and that you can walk over on a marked path.

The roads here are gentle but pleasant, with forest bends, farm lanes and village streets, and the surface is generally decent. Traffic is light, apart from pilgrims and walkers on summer weekends. Nowa Słupia has the basics, including small shops and places to eat, but not much else, and fuel is best done in Starachowice, eighteen kilometres away, a large town with all services. The village is quiet in winter, when the roads can be icy, and at its best in late spring and early autumn.
t.swiety krzyz@50.9,21.1:
The ridge called Łysa Góra, the Bald Mountain, has been climbed for a thousand years, and what the pilgrims are climbing to is the abbey of Święty Krzyż, the Holy Cross. The hill rises to roughly six hundred metres, which sounds modest until you see how it stands above the plain, with the dark fir and beech forest of the Świętokrzyskie National Park covering its flanks. The old Poles gave these hills a supernatural reputation: popular legend placed a witches' gathering on the bare summit, and some of the same folklore turns up in Polish literature, which is why you will find the name in unlikely places.

The abbey itself is Benedictine, and the tradition says it holds fragments of the wood of the Cross, brought here in the Middle Ages and venerated ever since. Kings and princes made the climb, and for centuries the monks were among the most powerful landowners in the region. The buildings have been burnt, rebuilt, plundered and put to strange uses: in the nineteenth century they served as a prison, and during the Second World War as a camp. Today the monks are back, and the courtyard is quiet and a little austere, with a view over forest in every direction.

What most visitors remember is the stone. Below the summit lies the gołoborze, a vast river of angular quartzite blocks that tumbles down the slope without a single tree growing on it. It was shaped in the cold of the last Ice Age, when frost split the rock, and the blocks have lain there ever since, covered in lichen and silent. A marked path crosses the field, and walking on it is oddly satisfying, though it is slippery after rain and not a place for riding boots with smooth soles.

The road up is a forest road, sometimes narrow and shaded, with bends that tighten as the gradient steepens, and a surface that is mostly good but can hold damp leaf litter and gravel. Parking close to the summit is limited, and you may find that the last stretch is done on foot, so check what is open on the day. Autumn is superb, with beeches the colour of copper, though weekends are crowded with school groups.
t.miko ajki lakes@53.8,21.6:
Mikołajki sits on a narrow neck of land between Lake Mikołajskie and Lake Tałty, and just south of it the huge, shallow expanse of Śniardwy opens out, the biggest lake in Poland. Everything here is water. The glaciers that scoured this part of the north-east left a maze of lakes joined by channels and rivers, and the town grew up as a fishing village where two of them touch. Today it calls itself the sailing capital of Masuria, and in July the harbour is a thicket of masts.

The best reason to swim here is that the lake is so unhurried. Water is shallow near the shore, warm by August, and clear enough that you see your feet. Public bathing spots are scattered around the town, along with the lakeside promenade and the old bridges that open for the passing yachts. A bronze whitefish king sits near the water, a bit of cheerful local mythology about a monarch of the fish who wore a crown, and children climb on it without apology. Fish is the thing to eat. Smoked eel, fried perch and pike-perch turn up on every menu, and the smoked varieties are sold from stalls near the quay.

Just a few kilometres away lies Łuknajno, a small lake that is a biosphere reserve and one of the best places in Europe to see mute swans in large numbers. It is a protected area, so you look from the edge and leave it alone. Cormorants, herons and cranes are common all across the region, and in the evening the call of a crane over reeds can stop a conversation.

The roads in the area are good, flat to gently rolling and often lined with old lime and chestnut trees that arch over the tarmac. They are lovely, but they are also full of tractors, delivery vans and holiday traffic on summer weekends, so treat them as a pleasant cruise rather than a challenge. Watch for deer at dusk and for speed cameras in the villages, where fifty means fifty. Mikołajki is large enough to have fuel stations and shops, and Mrągowo, a larger town about nineteen kilometres off, is the fallback. Come in June or early September if you can, when the lake is warm but the boardwalks are not yet shoulder to shoulder.
t.gizycko food@54.0,21.8:
Giżycko was once Lötzen, a small East Prussian town, and the name change tells you most of what happened to this region. It lies between two large lakes, Niegocin and Kisajno, on a narrow strip of land that has been fortified since the mid-nineteenth century. The star-shaped Boyen Fortress on the Niegocin side was built in the 1840s to guard the eastern border of Prussia. It never fought a great siege, which is perhaps why so much of it has survived, and you can walk along the earth ramparts and gate buildings at no great cost to your time.

The other landmark is the canal. A short waterway with a swing bridge connects the two lakes, and the bridge is turned by hand when boats pass, a bit of old machinery that still works and still holds up the traffic for a while. If you arrive at that moment, take it as a free pause. Sailors and canoeists fill the harbour all summer, and the town has a lively waterfront with ice cream stands and fish restaurants.

With almost thirty thousand people Giżycko is the busiest place on this ride, which is exactly why it is the right place to eat. Look for the local lake fish, zander or pike-perch with potatoes, or a bowl of sour rye żurek served in bread if the weather turns grey. Beer is cheap, and dumplings are everywhere. There are supermarkets, petrol stations on the main roads in and out, and a bike can be left in town without worry in the daytime.

The roads around town are flat and wooded, and the surface is variable. Fresh asphalt runs into patched seams, and bends tighten without much warning where a road follows a lake shore. Speed cameras and village limits are real, so stay within the signs. The Masurian summer is short and warm, September is calmer, and in mid-winter the lakes freeze hard enough for ice-sailing. If you have time for a short detour, Wolf's Lair, Hitler's wartime headquarters, lies in the forest near Kętrzyn, about half an hour away. It is a sombre ruin of concrete bunkers, and it sits very oddly among the birdsong and the ferns.
t.mragowo roads@53.9,21.3:
Mrągowo, the old Sensburg, is a lakeside town of about twenty-two thousand people in the heart of Warmia and Masuria, and the roads around it are the reason the ride exists. They are the kind that Poland does without trying: narrow country tarmac running between avenues of old lime, maple and ash, rising and dipping across moraine hills that the last ice age dumped here. Between the trees you catch flashes of small lakes, and in late afternoon the light comes in low through the leaves in a way that makes you slow down for no reason at all.

The town itself curls around Lake Czos, with a promenade, a beach, and an amphitheatre that hosts a big country music festival each summer. Yes, country music, in Poland, in the middle of the lakes. It has run for decades and draws a crowd that arrives by camper and tent. Outside festival time the place is quiet, with an old centre of modest size and some restored buildings from the Prussian period, when the region belonged to Germany and the town had a different name. Much of that history is gone, rewritten by the border changes of 1945.

For riding, think of the roads as relaxed rather than technical. The bends are mostly gentle, with the occasional tight one where a road drops to a lake or turns sharply in a village. Surface quality changes from smooth new asphalt to older patched sections, and you should expect gravel at the edges and the odd pothole after winter. Tractors are everywhere, and in a village the limit is fifty at any hour, with cameras and police who enjoy the rule. Deer and foxes come out at dusk, and storks nest on poles in the villages through summer.

Mrągowo is big enough for everything you need: fuel stations on the edge of town, grocery shops, pizzerias, kebab counters and a few places that serve decent Polish plates. If the weather is fine, buy something from a bakery and take it to the lake. If it rains, which it will sometimes, the roads get slick under the leaf litter, so slow down in autumn and watch the shaded corners.
t.kaliningrad@54.7,20.5:
Kaliningrad was once Königsberg, the capital of East Prussia, and what happened to it explains most of what you see. The city was heavily bombed in 1944 and fought over in 1945, then passed to the Soviet Union, its German population was expelled, and it was resettled and renamed in 1946. Today it is an exclave of Russia, cut off from the rest of the country by Lithuania and Poland, with its own character and a population of about four hundred thousand.

The great philosopher Immanuel Kant lived and died here and is buried against the wall of the cathedral on Kneiphof island, in the middle of the Pregel river. The cathedral was a ruin for decades and has been rebuilt as a museum and concert hall. Fragments of old Prussian gates and towers survive, and there are Soviet housing blocks beside them. The region is the world's largest source of amber, and the stone, fossilised tree resin about forty million years old, is sold in shops and displayed in a museum.

For riders the main attraction is the coast to the north and west. The Curonian Spit, a long, narrow sand peninsula, and the resort towns of Zelenogradsk and Svetlogorsk are reached by roads through forest and fields, and the Baltic is cold, grey and wide. Travel to and within Russia is subject to rules and sanctions that change, and anyone who might ride here needs to check entry requirements, border conditions and insurance carefully, since they may differ greatly from past years.

On the ground, the city has fuel stations and plenty of cafes. Local specialities include marzipan, which Königsberg was famous for, and fish from the Baltic. Summers are mild, winters cold and snowy. The roads are generally decent, though traffic into the city can jam. A walk around the island and the cathedral gives a sense of the layers of history in a place that has had many names.
t.ka fjord@70.0,23.1:
Kåfjord is a side arm of the Altafjord in Finnmark, and the little settlement on it lies just a few kilometres from Alta. It is a quiet place of birch, low farms and water, with the big mountains of the plateau standing behind. In the middle of the nineteenth century a copper mine operated here, financed by British investors, and the English managers brought a style of living that left a few odd traces in this far northern corner. The mine's story is a reminder that the Arctic coast was never as empty as the map suggests.

The fjord has a darker chapter too. In the Second World War the German battleship Tirpitz was based in these waters, hidden in the fjord arms to threaten Allied convoys to the Soviet Union, and the area was heavily fortified. Above the fjord on the mountain of Haldde stands an observatory built in the late nineteenth century, where the physicist Kristian Birkeland studied the northern lights. The aurora is still the reason many people come, and on a clear night between autumn and early spring the sky over Alta can flare green and violet.

The riding is easy and wide. The E6 leads in from the south and east, a fast, well-surfaced road that crosses the high plateau and drops toward the fjord, with long open views, little traffic and the constant chance of reindeer. In summer the sun does not set at all for weeks around midsummer, and you can ride through the small hours in warm, low light that makes the hillsides glow. Winter is another matter: the road is snow-packed, dark and often closed by storms, so this is a summer route unless you are well equipped.

Alta, about six kilometres away, is the place for fuel, food and supplies, and it has a big range of shops and cafes for the region. Nearby the Alta river is a famous salmon water, and the canyon upstream is one of the largest in northern Europe. If you have time, stand at the shore and watch the tide pull across the fjord, with the smell of seaweed and cold stone around you.
t.fuglenaes fuglenes@70.7,23.7:
Fuglenes is the headland at Hammerfest where one of Europe's long scientific ideas comes to an end. In the early nineteenth century the astronomer Friedrich Struve ran a chain of survey points stretching from the Black Sea to the Arctic Ocean to measure the shape of the Earth, and the northern end of that chain is marked here by a stone monument. It is a modest column on a rocky point, but it carries a World Heritage listing, and the idea of someone carrying a triangulation across ten countries makes you look at the little stone differently.

Hammerfest is often called the northernmost town in the world, a claim that depends on how you count, and it is one of the places that proudly says so anyway. It was among the first towns in Europe to have electric street lighting. In 1944 the retreating German army burned and destroyed nearly everything, so almost all the buildings are post-war, plain and practical, built in a hurry for people returning to nothing. The town's setting, with steep hills dropping into a harbour, is strong enough to carry it. Across the water the gas plant on Melkøya has become a feature of the skyline, and the polar bear society in the town hall is a curious little museum of Arctic hunting.

Getting here is a ride in itself. The road from Skaidi crosses the island of Kvaløya, climbs through bare tundra with scattered birches, and drops towards the sea with big views of the fjords. Surfaces are generally good but the weather can change quickly, with fog or wind coming off the Barents Sea, and in winter the road is often closed or convoy-driven. Reindeer are everywhere, standing on the tarmac in the long summer evenings, and you need to treat them as a regular hazard.

The town has fuel, shops and cafes, and the harbour has fish on the menu, often cod and Arctic char. Summer light lasts around the clock for weeks, which makes a late ride feel quite unreal, and in the darker months the northern lights are common over the harbour. Wrap up warmly even in July, because a wet wind from the north will cut through thin gear.
t.rock art of alta@70.0,23.2:
On the shore of the Altafjord, a few kilometres from the town, a long hill of smooth grey rock slopes down to the water, and its surface is covered with pictures. There are thousands of them, carved by hunters between roughly seven thousand and two thousand years ago: reindeer, elk, bears, boats, fish, and human figures that seem to dance or drum. The carvings sit at Hjemmeluft, beside the Alta Museum, and the whole group is a World Heritage site. The oldest are life-size reindeer, and some of the later scenes show hunting and ritual in strikingly lively detail.

A boardwalk runs over the rock so that you can look without walking on it. In summer the carvings were once painted red to help visitors see them, but they are best seen in low light, early or late, when the sun picks out the grooves. The sea level has fallen since they were made, so the older panels now sit higher up the hill, far from the water that those people knew. Standing among them with the fjord stretched below, you realise how short the distance is between that world and ours.

Alta has a recent history of its own. In the late 1970s and early 1980s a plan to dam the Alta river and flood the Sami village of Máze led to some of the biggest protests Norway has seen. The dam was built, though smaller than first intended, but the conflict helped lead to stronger recognition of Sami rights and a Sami parliament. The museum tells part of this story as well.

The riding to get here is the E6 across Finnmark, long, open and quiet, with a wide sky and the occasional reindeer in the road. In summer the midnight sun gives you light all night, and you can visit the carvings in the small hours if you like. Winter means snow, dark and ice, and a very different trip. Alta is only about four kilometres away and has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, so there is no need to plan around a gap. A coffee in the museum cafe is a good way to end.
t.rzeszow@50.0,22.0:
Rzeszów is the largest city in south-eastern Poland and the capital of the Podkarpackie region, a place that has grown fast and looks cheerful about it. The old market square has a Renaissance town hall and arcaded houses, and underneath it a network of cellars and passages has been opened to visitors as an underground route. The Lubomirski family built the castle that stands at the edge of the centre, and the area was long a crossroads of Polish, Ukrainian, Jewish and Carpathian culture. A strong aviation industry gives the city the nickname of the capital of Poland's Aviation Valley, and a fair number of its young people work in engineering.

For motorcyclists the city is an easy starting point for the Carpathian foothills. South of town the land rises steadily into wooded ridges, with the Bieszczady mountains and the Beskid Niski further off, and the roads become narrow and twisty, with villages of low wooden houses and old churches. The region is famous for its wooden churches, built from logs with shingled roofs and onion domes, and some of the oldest, such as the one at Haczów, are on the World Heritage list for the way they preserve medieval timber building. The rides here are linked to churches of this kind, including those dedicated to the Archangel Michael and the Assumption, which sit among orchards and fields on quiet back roads.

Autumn is a good season, with beech forests turning gold and mist in the valleys, and the summer is warm but rarely oppressive. Roads in Poland vary, with the main routes in good condition and the smaller ones patched and sometimes rough, and speed limits in villages are enforced firmly by cameras and police. Take care at dusk, as deer, farm vehicles and cyclists without lights are common on the country roads.

Fuel is no problem in Rzeszów, with stations all over the ring road and the A4 motorway that passes the city. About seventeen kilometres east, the castle at Łańcut is a fine stop, and its gardens and carriage museum make a pleasant break. For lunch, look for pierogi or a bowl of żurek, the soured rye soup, in one of the simple restaurants on the market square.
t.inawashiro@37.6,140.1:
Inawashiro lies at the foot of Mount Bandai, on the northern shore of the lake that shares its name, in Fukushima Prefecture. The lake, the fourth largest in Japan, is a wide sheet of clear water, and it is known for its colour, an unusually deep blue, partly because the water is slightly acidic and low in nutrients. In winter, whooper swans arrive from Siberia and gather near the shore, and with the snow-covered cone of Bandai above them, it is one of the great winter scenes in northern Honshu.

The town has a few notable claims. Hideyo Noguchi, the bacteriologist who became world-famous in the early twentieth century for his research on yellow fever and syphilis, was born in a farmhouse here, and a museum recalls his life. The old farmer's house of the era, with its central hearth, is preserved. Bandai itself erupted catastrophically in 1888, when the north face collapsed and flattened villages, and the debris created the lakes and marshes of the Urabandai plateau, among them the colourful Goshiki-numa ponds. The scars are visible on the mountain's shape.

For motorcyclists, Inawashiro is a gateway. The Bandai-Azuma Skyline, a high mountain road that climbs from Fukushima toward the Azuma range, passes through volcanic landscape with steaming vents and grand views, and it is among the best-known roads in Tohoku. It is closed in winter, usually from November until April, so check dates, and in summer the weather can switch from sun to fog in minutes. The Bandai Gold Line and the roads around Lake Hibara are also very good, with fine bends and scenery.

Inawashiro has stations, shops and cafes, and it is the sensible place to refill before the mountains. Aizu, to the west, is known for its castle, its lacquerware and its cold noodles. Try the local ramen, Kitakata style, a short drive away, or a bowl of soba. Lake views at dusk, with lights on the water, close a long day well.
t.mission valero@29.4,-98.5:
San Antonio de Valero is the formal name of what the world knows as the Alamo. The mission was founded in 1718 by Spanish Franciscans, who named it in honor of Saint Anthony of Padua and the viceroy of New Spain, the Marqués de Valero. It stood beside the San Antonio River, on land that offered water, irrigation and a place to teach indigenous families a farming life. By the end of the eighteenth century the mission was secularized, and its old chapel became a military post, whose name came from the Spanish word for cottonwood.

Its modern fame comes from the thirteen days in 1836 when a small group of Texan defenders, among them Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie, held out against the Mexican army of General Santa Anna. All of the defenders died on the final morning, and the cry of Remember the Alamo became the rallying cry of the Texas Revolution. Visitors often arrive expecting a large fortress and are surprised to find a small stone chapel with its famous curved parapet, sitting among tall buildings in the middle of downtown.

Riding here is an urban business. Alamo Plaza is a busy pedestrian area beside the River Walk, which winds beneath the street level in a green channel of restaurants and shade. The streets around it are narrow and often one-way, and parking can be slow and costly, though motorcycles can sometimes find a spot more easily. Visit on a weekday morning, since weekends and holidays bring crowds and heat. In the summer, the sun is relentless, and humidity can make the downtown feel like a sauna.

The wider San Antonio Missions are the best reason to come. Four more missions run south along the river, and together with the Alamo they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015. Their ride is a pleasant one on the old Mission Road and the river trail, with live oaks, cottonwoods and old stone churches.

Fuel and food are no problem. The city has stations in every direction and a good supply of Tex-Mex, barbecue and breakfast tacos that rank among the best anywhere. If you need a restful pause, sit in the Alamo's gardens, which are shaded and quiet.
t.mission concepcion@29.4,-98.5:
Mission Concepción is the quiet one, and many people think it is the best preserved. Its full name is Nuestra Señora de la Purísima Concepción de Acuña, and its stone church was completed in the 1750s, which makes it the oldest unrestored stone church in the United States still in use. It stands on a low rise a few miles south of downtown San Antonio, with two bell towers, a dome and a facade that is plain but beautifully proportioned. The Franciscans moved the mission here in 1731 from East Texas, where drought and conflict had driven them out, and here they found the river and a better chance.

Inside you can still see the traces of the original frescoes, with geometric patterns in faded reds and ochres on the walls and ceiling of the sacristy. The colors were applied with natural pigments and have lasted far longer than anyone expected. It is a chance to see how the mission interiors were meant to look, bright and decorated rather than bare stone, and it is more touching than grand. The mission also saw fighting in 1835, when a small Texan force defeated a larger Mexican detachment in the Battle of Concepción, a prelude to the siege at the Alamo.

The ride is easy and urban. The Mission Trail follows South Mission Road and then the river, with the old acequia irrigation ditches visible in places. Streets are shaded by live oaks and the traffic is moderate outside rush hour. Be aware that summers in San Antonio are very hot, with temperatures often in the high thirties Celsius, and the best hours are early morning or late afternoon. In winter, a cold front can drop the temperature suddenly and bring a light ice.

Mission Concepción is still a working parish church, so visitors are asked to be quiet and respectful, particularly during services. The grounds are open, and there is a small visitor center run by the National Park Service. Entry is free. A bench in the shade of the courtyard is a good place to sit and listen to the sounds of the city fade.

Fuel and food are close by. San Antonio has stations everywhere, and Southtown to the north has cafes and bakeries. Try a pan dulce and coffee before you move on.
t.mission san jose@29.4,-98.5:
Mission San José is known as the Queen of the Missions, and it earns the title. Founded in 1720, it grew into the largest and most complete of the San Antonio missions, a walled community with a church, granary, workshops, a mill and rows of small apartments for the indigenous families who lived inside. The compound still has much of its outer wall, and walking through the gate gives a sense of the size of the settlement. The church is the centerpiece, built in the late eighteenth century with a facade of carved limestone that is more ornate than anything else in the city.

The best-known detail is the Rose Window, a small, intricately carved opening on the side of the sacristy, which legend ties to the sculptor Pedro Huizar and to a love story, though the truth is harder to pin down. The stonework around the main doorway is full of scrollwork, saints and floral carvings, and the whole facade seems to glow in the late afternoon sun. The granary and the working gristmill, partly restored, show how the mission fed itself, and an old irrigation ditch still runs along one side.

The ride to San José is a pleasant stretch along the Mission Trail. South of downtown, Roosevelt Avenue and Mission Road take you past residential streets, old trees and a few old stone buildings. The San Antonio River Walk extends here in a quieter, more natural form called the Mission Reach, and you can see herons, turtles and the occasional egret from the bank. Summers are hot and humid, and the best time to ride is early or late in the day. A morning visit means softer light and fewer visitors.

The mission is part of San Antonio Missions National Historical Park, and it is also a living parish, with services held in the church. Visitors should act accordingly. A small visitor center has maps and a short film. Entry to the grounds is free, though special tours and events may have fees.

Fuel and food are easy to find along Roosevelt Avenue, and nearby neighborhoods have plenty of Mexican bakeries and taquerias. Stop for a plate of barbacoa or a fresh tortilla, and you have the taste of the place.
t.bandai azuma skyline point 3@37.7,140.2:
The high ground of the Bandai-Azuma Skyline is a lunar landscape, and you reach it after the forest drops away and the road emerges onto bare, gravelly slopes of volcanic rock. Here, at around 1,600 metres, the Azuma volcanic group stands around you, with craters, steaming vents and scoured ridges, and the famous Mount Issaikyo, which still releases gas from its crater. On a clear day, the views stretch across the whole range and down to the plains. This is the highest and most exposed part of the road, with wind that can be fierce.

The area known as Jododaira is the main stop, with a visitor centre, a car park, and walking trails that lead to the crater rim. Short walks take you across the black cinders to viewpoints, and in early summer the slopes are covered with alpine flowers. Mountain climbers use this as a gateway to higher routes. The air is thin, cool and clean, and in summer it can be twenty degrees cooler than the city below.

The Skyline here is a pleasure on a motorbike. The road is smooth and wide, with open bends, long views and little traffic, apart from tourist buses and sightseeing cars. Heavy mist and strong winds can come with little warning, so the road can be hazardous in poor weather. Gas fumes sometimes affect the road near the vents, and warnings are posted. In winter, the road is closed by deep snow, and in spring the snow walls on both sides of the road are a famous sight.

The visitor centre has a small restaurant with simple meals, and vending machines are everywhere in Japan, selling hot coffee, even in remote places. Bring a windproof jacket, even in summer, and give the weather a chance to clear before you go on.
t.bandai azuma skyline point 4@37.7,140.3:
At the southern end of the Skyline, the road leaves the barren high ground and comes down into a gentler landscape of forest, lakes and wide views toward Mount Bandai. This is the part of Fukushima prefecture that surrounds Lake Inawashiro, the fourth-largest lake in Japan, and the land is dotted with hot springs, ski resorts and small farms. Mount Bandai itself is a famous volcano, and its great collapse in 1888 buried villages and dammed rivers, forming the lakes and ponds of the Urabandai area, which now look like a scatter of coloured jewels in the forest.

The road here is easy and relaxed after the high section, with long, sweeping descents and gentle bends through cedar and beech forest. Autumn brings a bright flush of red and orange, and the combination of volcanic landscape and forest is famous. Surface conditions are good, but fallen leaves and damp patches can reduce grip. Rain is common in summer, and fog can settle in the valleys.

Inawashiro and Nihommatsu are the nearest towns of any size, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Inawashiro is also the birthplace of Hideyo Noguchi, a bacteriologist whose face appeared on the thousand-yen note for two decades, and a museum there tells his story. In the Aizu region nearby, the old castle town of Aizuwakamatsu has a fine castle and a samurai heritage connected with the Boshin war of the 1860s, when local warriors fought on the losing side against the new imperial government.

Local food includes soba noodles, miso-glazed grilled rice balls and Aizu sake. The region is cold in winter, with heavy snow, and the roads close on the upper sections. For riders, the best months are May to October. If the sky is clear, pull over where you can see Bandai, whose broken, crater-scarred shape is a reminder of what the mountain did.
t.norwegian scenic route havoysund point 1:
Out here the road to Havøysund begins to feel like the edge of the map. This is Finnmark, the northernmost county of Norway, and the land is a rolling plateau of bare rock, bog, low birch scrub and small lakes, with no tall trees to break the wind. The road leaves the main highway near Skaidi and heads north across the tundra, and the sense of space is powerful: low hills fade into each other, the sky is huge and the light has a clear, hard quality. In summer the sun does not set for weeks, and in winter it vanishes entirely.

This is Sámi country, and reindeer herders have used these plateaus for centuries, driving their animals between winter pastures inland and summer pastures on the coast. In summer the reindeer are often on or beside the road, standing in the lane with the calm of animals that own the place, and the right response is to slow down, stop if necessary and wait for them to move. Cars and bikes have no priority here. The animals can appear suddenly over a rise, and a collision is bad for both parties.

The riding is simple but memorable. The road is generally good, with wide curves, gentle gradients and very little traffic, and the long horizons let you see a vehicle coming a long way off. Wind is the main hazard, and even in July the temperature can be low, with cold rain and fog arriving suddenly from the Barents Sea. A warm layer, waterproofs and gloves are not optional. Late evening in midsummer, when the sun skims along the horizon, gives the best light.

Distances are large and settlements few. Hammerfest, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest town of size and a sensible place to fill the tank and stock up on food before the northern run. Take a drink and a snack in your tank bag, and stop sometimes just to look. The silence on this plateau is deep, broken only by the wind and the occasional call of a bird.
t.norwegian scenic route havoysund point 2:
Halfway along the Havøysund road the land begins to tilt toward the sea. The plateau is lower here, the lakes are bigger and the first fjords start to cut into the coast, with long inlets of cold, dark water between rounded hills. The vegetation is thin, a few birches in sheltered hollows and otherwise heather, lichen and dwarf shrubs, and in autumn the whole landscape turns red and gold with astonishing intensity. In summer the cotton grass makes white patches in the bogs.

The wildlife is more varied than the bare land suggests. Reindeer wander in herds on the hills, arctic foxes and ptarmigan live in the uplands, and the coast is rich in seabirds, including eiders, gulls, and the occasional sea eagle. The Barents Sea is cold but productive, and the fisheries of Finnmark have fed the coast for a thousand years. Cod and haddock are the staple, and the long wooden racks used to dry fish in the wind are still seen in some places.

Finnmark's history is marked by the war. In the autumn of 1944, as German forces retreated before the Soviet advance, they burned most of the settlements in the county and forced the population to leave, so much of the north was rebuilt from nothing after 1945. Many of the villages therefore look plain and modern, built for practicality, with little of the old wooden charm found farther south. It is a part of the story that is rarely mentioned in the glossy brochures, but it gives the place a particular seriousness.

The road here is quiet and rewarding, with long straights and sweeping views, and the surface is generally smooth. Take care in wet weather, and keep a lookout for reindeer. Ávanuorri, the community at the end of the road, is some twenty-three kilometres ahead, and Hammerfest is a good deal farther behind, so keep your fuel and supplies in mind. In the long summer evenings it is possible to ride late and see the land in a very low, golden light.
t.hammerfest@70.7,23.7:
Hammerfest likes to call itself the northernmost town in the world, a title it has argued over for years with Honningsvåg further east, depending on how you define a town. Either way, you are a long way up: at seventy degrees north, on the island of Kvaløya, with the Barents Sea around the corner and a winter in which the sun does not rise above the horizon for about two months. In summer it does the opposite, and from mid-May to late July the midnight sun circles the sky without setting.

The town has had a hard history. It was a trading post for centuries, a base for Arctic fishing and hunting, and in 1891 it became the first town in Northern Europe to have electric street lighting, powered by its own hydroelectric plant. Then, in late 1944, the retreating German army burned Hammerfest to the ground as part of a scorched-earth policy across Finnmark, and the population was forcibly evacuated. Almost nothing survived except a small chapel in the cemetery. Today's town is a post-war rebuild, practical and colourful rather than old, and the local reconstruction museum tells the story well. On the headland stands the Meridian Column, a monument to the Struve Geodetic Arc, a nineteenth-century survey chain now listed by UNESCO.

The ride in is a long spur from the E6. You leave the main road at Skaidi and follow route 94 out across the treeless tundra and along the fjord, around sixty kilometres of gentle, well-kept road with reindeer wandering on and off the tarmac, so stay alert. The landscape is bare and rolling, with lichen, rock and water, and the wind can be relentless. Even in July, bring proper layers and waterproofs, because a sunny afternoon can turn to sleet in an hour.

Hammerfest has everything a rider needs after a long northern stage: fuel, supermarkets, cafes, hotels and a hospital, and it is the last town of this size before the long haul to the North Cape. The local economy now leans heavily on gas: the Melkøya liquefied natural gas plant just offshore processes gas from the Snøhvit field under the Barents Sea, and its flare stack is a strange sight at night. Fill the tank here, eat something hot, and check the forecast for the tundra crossing.
t.near avanuorri@70.9,24.7:
The last kilometres of the road to Havøysund run across one of the barest landscapes in Norway, a coast of grey rock, heather and lichen, with the Barents Sea on one side and nothing taller than a person for miles. Ávanuorri is the Sami name for Havøysund, the fishing village at the end of the road, and this point lies just before you reach it, on the open stretch where the road makes its final run toward the village.

The Havøysund route is one of the more remote National Tourist Routes in Norway, branching off the main road near Kokelv and running northwest along the coast for about seventy kilometres. It passes old fishing settlements, sheltered bays and long, empty stretches of shore where the only signs of life are reindeer, which graze along the coast in summer, and seabirds. The road was only completed in the twentieth century, and before that the communities here were reached by boat. There is a rest stop at Selvika, with a curving wooden walkway down to the beach.

The riding is not technical, but it is atmospheric. The road follows the shore, with short climbs, gentle bends and long views, and the surface is generally decent, although frost heave and patching are normal this far north. The wind is the biggest factor, sometimes strong enough to push the bike sideways, and the weather can change quickly from clear to fog. In June and July the sun never sets, and the light at midnight on this coast is extraordinary. Watch out for reindeer on the road, which do not move quickly and sometimes not at all.

Havøysund, a few minutes away, has the services for this end of the route: a shop, a cafe or two, fuel and accommodation. There is little else for many kilometres, so make sure the tank is healthy when you leave the main road. If the weather is kind, ride the route out in the evening and back in the small hours, when the low sun turns the rock pink and you may have the whole coast to yourself.
t.avanuorri@71.0,24.7:
Havøysund, Ávanuorri in Sami, is a fishing village at the very end of a road at the top of Norway, in Måsøy municipality, where the land runs out into the Barents Sea. It is a working place, not a pretty one: a harbour with fishing boats, a fish processing plant, rows of houses painted in bright colours against the grey rock, and a sense that the people here have chosen to live with the weather rather than fight it. The Hurtigruten coastal ships call here on their way between Hammerfest and Honningsvåg.

The village has a hard history. Like almost every settlement in Finnmark, it was burned by the retreating German army in 1944, when the population was forcibly evacuated and the whole region was scorched to deny shelter to the advancing Soviet forces. After the war people came back and rebuilt, and the houses you see date from that time, plain and practical. Fishing, especially for cod and other whitefish, has always been the basis of life here.

Above the village, on the island of Havøya, the Havøygavlen wind farm stands on the ridge, and there is a hiking path up to the top that gives a fine view over the sea and the coast. In summer, the light never fades, and on clear evenings the sun hangs over the northern horizon. Seabirds nest along the cliffs, and if you are lucky you may see sea eagles, which are common along this coast.

The road here is the end of the Havøysund National Tourist Route, about seventy kilometres from the main road at Kokelv, and there is no way onward except by boat. That makes it a ride for its own sake: you come for the empty coast, the wind and the sense of reaching an edge. The road is open all year, but in winter storms can close it for periods.

Havøysund has a shop, fuel, a cafe and accommodation, which is fortunate, because there is little else for a long way. Fill up before starting back, and keep an eye out for reindeer on the way.
t.kashima shi@36.0,140.6:
Kashima's great shrine claims to be one of the oldest in Japan, and its deity, Takemikazuchi, is a god of thunder and swords. A stone in the shrine forest, the kaname-ishi, is said to pin down the head of a giant catfish beneath the earth whose thrashing causes earthquakes. Only a small rounded top shows above ground; legend says that no amount of digging has ever reached its bottom. The forest around the shrine, with tall cedars, deer and a spring-fed pond, is a cool, dark refuge on a summer day.

The town itself is a mix of industry and sport. A huge steelworks and petrochemical complex dominates the coast, built around a deep artificial harbour, and the Kashima Antlers, one of the most successful clubs in Japanese football, play at a stadium on the edge of town.

To the east, the Kashima-nada coast runs for tens of kilometres, a long, straight beach of sand and surf facing the open Pacific. Swimming is popular in July and August, when designated beaches open with lifeguards, but the waves can be powerful and rip currents strong. Outside the official season, the beaches are the domain of surfers and fishermen.

West of the town, the shores of Kitaura and the wider Kasumigaura lake system offer flat, quiet roads through rice fields and lotus ponds. In summer the lotus flowers bloom, and herons stalk the paddies.

The approach street to the shrine has old tea houses selling sweet dumplings, which is the civilised way to take a break; for fuel and a cold can, the national road through town has the usual stations and konbini.
t.near oami on the way back@35.5,140.2:
It is farming country: rice paddies, vegetable fields, greenhouses and patches of woodland, with low hills to the south and a scattering of small towns. Chiba is famous for its peanuts, and in autumn the fields are dotted with drying stacks, called bocchi, a sight unique to this part of Japan.

East of here, beyond Ōami, lies Kujūkuri beach, one of the longest beaches in Japan, stretching for roughly sixty kilometres along the Pacific coast. It is a broad, flat beach of fine sand, with powerful surf and strong currents. Swimming is allowed at designated beaches during the official season in July and August, with lifeguards and flags. Outside the season or the flagged zones, the sea can be dangerous, and drownings occur every year.

The Kujūkuri toll road runs behind the dunes along the coast, a straight, quiet road with views of the sea and the pine forests that protect the land from the wind and sand. It is not challenging riding, but it is relaxing, with little traffic and a cool sea breeze.

Inland, the roads are flat and straight, running between fields and through small towns. Watch for slow farm vehicles, sudden junctions and cyclists. The hills to the south, around Mobara and Ichihara, offer more interesting roads, with gentle bends and wooded slopes.

Grilled clams, hamaguri, are what the Kujūkuri coast is known for, eaten hot from the shell at roadside shacks in season. Ōami and Mobara cover fuel and convenience stores; out in the fields, do not assume the next village will have a pump.
t.ohara@35.2,140.4:
Every September the men of Ōhara carry portable shrines straight into the Pacific, running through the surf to the beat of drums in a festival that has been held for centuries. It is a wild, joyful sight, and it sums up this small fishing town on the eastern coast of the Boso peninsula, where life still revolves around the sea and the boats.

Ōhara is part of Isumi city, and its harbour lands some of the largest catches of Japanese spiny lobster, ise-ebi, in the country. In season, the restaurants near the port serve it grilled, boiled or in miso soup, along with whatever else the boats brought in that morning. It is a good place to eat, and lunch here is reason enough to stop.

The Isumi railway, a little single-track local line, runs inland from Ōhara through rice fields and wooded hills. In spring, rapeseed flowers bloom along the tracks, and the small yellow trains pass through a sea of colour. Railway fans travel from all over Japan to photograph it.

The coast road south towards Katsuura is a pleasant ride, with views over rocky bays and small beaches, and Katsuura's morning market, one of the most famous in Japan, has been held for over four hundred years. Inland, the roads wind through quiet valleys with little traffic, and the hills are green and wooded.

The town covers the basics, pumps and konbini included. Beaches along this stretch open for swimming in July and August, but the Pacific does not do gentle here; stay between the flags and leave the reef edges to the surfers.
t.near minamiboso on the way back@35.0,140:
At Nojimazaki, the southern tip of the Boso peninsula, a white lighthouse stands on a rocky point above the Pacific. It was one of the first Western-style lighthouses in Japan, built in the late 1860s by a French engineer, and its gallery looks out over a coast of black rocks, surf and wide horizons. The stop sits a little way inland, in the hills between Minamibōsō and Tateyama.

The southern Boso has a mild climate, warmed by the Kuroshio current, and flowers bloom here in the depths of winter. The Boso Flower Line, the coast road from Tateyama to Shirahama, runs past fields of rapeseed, stock and poppies, and in January and February, when the rest of Japan is cold and grey, the fields are a riot of colour.

Shirahama is the home of the ama, women divers who for centuries have gathered abalone, turban shells and seaweed from the seabed without breathing gear. Their tradition is celebrated in a summer festival, when the divers carry torches into the sea at night.

For a swim, the beaches around Shirahama and the southern coast are open in July and August, with lifeguards and flags. The surf can be strong on the Pacific side, so swim only in designated areas.

The riding on the southern Boso is gentle and scenic, with coast roads, hills and little traffic outside the holiday season. The roads inland are narrow and winding, with forests and small villages. Tateyama, twenty minutes up the coast, handles fuel. Down here, eat where the boats tie up: the small harbour restaurants serve whatever came in that morning, often with a view of the divers' huts.
t.near honcho@35.7,140.0:
Honchō is the central district of Funabashi, a big commuter city on the northern shore of Tokyo Bay in Chiba Prefecture. This is not riding country in itself; it is the urban sprawl you have to pass through to get from Tokyo towards the mountains and coasts beyond, and the best attitude is patience and a full tank.

Funabashi has been a stop on the road for centuries. During the Edo period it was a post town on the routes leading east from the capital, and its old shrine, Funabashi Daijingū, is said to be very old. Today the city is a dense mix of apartments, shopping streets, railway lines and expressways, with the vast Lalaport shopping complex and the Sanbanze tidal flats on the bay, where shellfish gatherers still work and migratory birds gather. The area is also known for its nashi pears, sold in late summer at roadside stands on the outskirts.

Riding here means traffic lights, scooters, delivery vans and lane splitting by locals. Routes 14 and 357 run along the bay, while the Keiyō Road and the Higashi-Kantō Expressway offer faster escapes. Expressways are tolled, and ETC cards make the process smoother, though cash lanes still exist. Summer heat and humidity can be oppressive in stop-start traffic, so plan an early departure.

Fuel stations are plentiful, many of them self-service, others with attendants who will guide you in, fill up and even wipe your mirror. Convenience stores are everywhere and make great rest stops, with coffee, onigiri and clean toilets. Take a break here, check your route, and head out towards the Bōsō Peninsula or north towards the mountains of Tochigi and Fukushima, where the real riding begins.
t.near ichihara@35.6,140.0:
A layer of rock in a riverbank near Ichihara has given its name to a slice of Earth's history. In 2020, the international body that decides such things named a geological age the Chibanian, after a cliff on the Yōrō river where the last reversal of the Earth's magnetic field is recorded with unusual clarity. The site is small and muddy, reached by a short path, but standing in front of it is a strange experience, a few hundred thousand years of time in a single bank of clay.

Ichihara itself is a big city stretching from the industrial shoreline of Tokyo Bay, lined with refineries and petrochemical plants, deep into the rural hills of central Chiba. The inland part is a world away from the coast: rolling hills, rice terraces, forests and small villages. The Kominato Railway, a charming local line with old diesel trains, winds through the valleys and is especially beautiful during the cherry and rapeseed blossom season.

For riders, the inland roads are the highlight. The Yōrō valley, further south, is famous for its gorges, waterfalls and autumn colours, and the roads that wind through it are narrow, twisting and fun. The hills of the Bōsō peninsula are low, but they have plenty of curves and little traffic outside weekends. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel and leaves on the corners.

Ichihara has fuel, konbini-style convenience stores and plenty of places to eat. The roadside stations in the hills offer local produce and snacks, and the onsen of the Yōrō valley are a good place to relax after a day of riding. The view across the hills, with layers of ridges fading into the distance, makes the climb worthwhile.
t.near kisarazu@35.3,140.0:
Kisarazu is the Chiba end of the Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line, and for riders that alone makes it special. The Aqua-Line crosses the bay from Kawasaki in two halves: a long tunnel under the water, then a low bridge that skims across the surface for several kilometres into Kisarazu. In the middle sits Umihotaru, an artificial island with a parking area, restaurants and a deck with views over the bay, where on a clear day you can see Mount Fuji to the west and the towers of Tokyo and Yokohama to the north. It is tolled, and crosswinds on the bridge section can be fierce.

The town itself is an old port on the eastern shore of the bay. Its tidal flats are known for clam digging, shiohigari, a favourite family outing in spring and early summer, and asari clams turn up in local dishes. The temple of Shojoji is associated with a well-known folk song about dancing tanuki, the mischievous raccoon dogs of Japanese legend, and you will find tanuki statues around the town.

As a food stop and finish, Kisarazu has plenty to offer, from seafood restaurants near the harbour to family restaurants and convenience stores along the main roads. A bowl of clam ramen or a seafood rice bowl makes a fine end to a day.

The roads inland from Kisarazu lead into the Boso hills, with winding routes through forests and small valleys towards the Pacific coast. The hills are low but steep, and the roads can be narrow and twisting. Traffic is heavy around the Aqua-Line approaches on weekends, especially in the evening, when everyone heads back to Tokyo. Fuel is plentiful.
t.near mitsukaido@36.0,140.0:
Mitsukaidō, now part of the city of Jōsō in south-western Ibaraki, lies on the vast, flat Kanto plain north of Tokyo, beside the Kinugawa river. The landscape is one of rice paddies, irrigation channels, farmhouses with windbreak trees and long river embankments, under a big sky. To the north-east, Mount Tsukuba rises alone from the plain, its twin peaks visible from far away, and on clear winter days Mount Fuji can sometimes be seen far to the south-west.

The Kinugawa is usually a placid river, but in September 2015, heavy rains caused its embankment to break in Jōsō, flooding a large part of the city and forcing thousands of people to evacuate. The flood was one of the worst in recent Japanese history, and the embankments have since been rebuilt and strengthened. Riding along them today, it is hard to imagine the water spreading across the plain.

The paddies change with the seasons: flooded and mirror-like in spring, when rice is planted; lush and green in summer; golden in early autumn, before the harvest; and bare and brown in winter. Herons and egrets stalk the fields, and in the evening the croaking of frogs fills the air.

For riders, the plain offers flat, straight roads, with long views and little traffic away from the main routes. The embankment roads along the rivers are often scenic, though some are restricted to cyclists and pedestrians. Fuel and food are available in Jōsō and the surrounding towns. As a photo stop, the paddies with Mount Tsukuba in the background are lovely, especially at sunrise or sunset.
t.near ishige@36.1,140.1:
Ishige is a rural district of south-western Ibaraki, now part of the city of Jōsō, on the Kanto plain between the Kinugawa and Kokai rivers. It is a gentle, open landscape of rice paddies, vegetable fields, groves of trees around old farmhouses and shrines in small woods, with Mount Tsukuba standing alone on the horizon to the north-east.

This area is part of the old Shimōsa and Hitachi provinces, and in the tenth century it was the stronghold of Taira no Masakado, a warrior who rebelled against the imperial court and declared himself the new emperor in the east. His rebellion was crushed and he was killed in 940, but he became a legend, and shrines dedicated to him are found across the Kanto region, including the famous Kanda Myōjin in Tokyo. His spirit was long believed to be powerful and vengeful.

As a food stop, the area offers the simple pleasures of rural Japan. Roadside michi-no-eki rest areas sell local vegetables, rice, sweets and bento, and restaurants serve soba, udon and tonkatsu. Ibaraki is known for its melons, chestnuts and natto, fermented soybeans, which are an acquired taste but a source of local pride.

The riding is flat and relaxed, with straight roads through the paddies and along the rivers, and very little traffic away from the main routes. Fuel and food are available in Jōsō and the surrounding towns. The views of Mount Tsukuba across the fields are lovely, especially in the morning light.
t.near kisarazu@35.5,140.0:
North of Kisarazu, the flat industrial shore of Tokyo Bay gives way inland to the Boso hills, a rumpled landscape of low, steep ridges and narrow valleys covered in forest. The hills are not high, but they are surprisingly wild, cut by deep ravines and rivers that wind through them in tight loops, and they offer some of the best riding close to Tokyo.

The Yōrō river is the star. Its valley, the Yōrō Keikoku, is a gorge of sandstone cliffs, waterfalls and forests, especially beautiful in late November and early December, when the maples turn red and gold. Awamata Falls, a long, shallow cascade over a rock slope, is one of the most popular spots. The Kominato Railway, a rural line with old diesel trains, runs through the valley, and its little wooden stations are charming.

As a high point, the ridges above the gorge offer views over the folded hills, with the bay and the industrial shore visible in the distance. On clear days, Mount Fuji can be seen far to the west, across the bay.

For riders, the roads through the Boso hills are a joy: narrow, twisting, with short climbs and descents, and generally light traffic, except in the foliage season. Surfaces vary, and some roads are narrow, with blind corners and gravel. Watch for wildlife, including deer, monkeys and wild boar. Fuel and food are available in Kisarazu, Ichihara and the small towns in the hills, but stations are sparse in the interior, so fill up before you go.
t.near honcho@35.6,140.0:
Along the north-eastern shore of Tokyo Bay, between Funabashi and Chiba, almost everything you see stands on land that did not exist a century ago. Reclamation turned tidal flats and shallow water into ports, factories, housing and the business district of Makuhari, with its convention centre, Makuhari Messe, and the stadium of the Chiba Lotte Marines baseball team. Inage, a little further south, has an artificial beach with a promenade and views across the bay.

The shore was once famous for its tidal flats, where people dug for clams and gathered seaweed, and the fishermen of the bay supplied Edo with fresh seafood. Most of that has gone, but a few patches survive, including the Yatsu tidal flat in Narashino, protected as a wetland of international importance and a haven for migratory birds.

As a finishing stretch, this coast is about getting home. The Keiyō road and the Higashi-Kantō expressway run along the shore, carrying heavy traffic towards Tokyo, and the local roads are busy and lined with traffic lights. But in the evening, with the sun setting over the bay and the towers of Tokyo glowing on the horizon, there is a certain urban beauty to it, and on clear days Mount Fuji appears on the far side of the water.

Fuel and food are plentiful along the shore. The promenades at Makuhari and Inage are pleasant places to stop and watch the sunset before the last stretch home.
t.near sakura@35.7,140.2:
Sakura, in northern Chiba, was a castle town in the Edo period, and some of its old samurai residences survive on a quiet street, with thatched roofs and earthen walls, giving a glimpse of how the warrior class lived. The castle itself is gone, but its grounds now house the National Museum of Japanese History, one of the best museums in the country, covering everything from prehistoric times to the twentieth century.

Just outside the town, beside the lake of Inba-numa, stands a Dutch-style windmill, surrounded by tulip fields that bloom in brilliant colour in April. The windmill commemorates Sakura's historical links with Dutch learning, rangaku, which flourished here in the Edo period. The Kawamura Memorial DIC Museum of Art, set in a park nearby, has a fine collection of modern art, including a room of paintings by Mark Rothko.

The landscape around Sakura is a gentle mix of low hills, rice paddies, woods and lakes, and it makes for pleasant, relaxed riding. The roads around Inba-numa are flat and open, with views over the water, and the routes through the hills are winding and wooded. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, especially near Narita airport, but the minor roads are quiet.

As a start and finish, Sakura offers a calm, cultural setting, with plenty of places to eat and drink. Fuel is available in town. The lake at sunset, with the windmill silhouetted against the sky, is a lovely way to end the day.
t.near mobara@35.4,140.1:
Mobara is a quiet city in central Chiba, on the eastern side of the Boso Peninsula, where the low hills of the interior meet the long, straight coast of Kujūkuri Beach. The landscape is a gentle mix of rice paddies, woods and small towns, with the hills rising gradually to the south and west.

A few kilometres north-west, at Chōnan, stands one of the most unusual temples in Japan. Kasamori-dera is built on top of a rocky outcrop, supported by a forest of wooden pillars, in a style that is said to be unique in the country. Climbing the steep stairs to the veranda gives you a view over the surrounding forest. To the east, Kujūkuri Beach stretches for some sixty kilometres along the Pacific, one of the longest beaches in Japan, popular with surfers.

The riding around Mobara is relaxed and pleasant. The roads through the hills are winding and wooded, with short climbs and descents, and the routes along the coast are flat and open, with the sea on one side and pine forests on the other. Traffic is light away from the main roads, though summer weekends bring crowds to the beach.

Mobara has fuel, food and basic services. As a start and finish, it offers a calm setting on the quieter side of the Boso Peninsula. The hills to the south, around Ōtaki and Isumi, offer more interesting riding through forests and valleys.
t.near ami@36.0,140.2:
Ami is a town in southern Ibaraki on the western shore of Kasumigaura, the second-largest lake in Japan, a broad, shallow sheet of water fringed with reeds, lotus fields and fishing villages. The land around it is flat to gently rolling, with fields, woods and scattered settlements, and Mount Tsukuba rises to the north-west, the only real mountain for miles.

Ami has a sobering place in Japanese history. During the Second World War, the Imperial Navy trained young pilots here, at the Kasumigaura naval air base and the Yokaren preparatory flight school, and many of them later died in the Pacific, some in kamikaze attacks. The Yokaren Peace Memorial Museum in Ami tells their story with letters, photographs and personal belongings, and it is a quiet, moving place.

Just to the south, in Ushiku, stands one of the largest statues in the world: the Ushiku Daibutsu, a bronze Buddha well over a hundred metres tall, rising above the surrounding fields. It is visible for miles, and you can take a lift up inside it to a viewing platform. Seeing it appear on the horizon as you ride is a surreal experience.

As a high point, the term is relative: the land is low, and the views are of the lake and the plain. But the lakeside roads offer long views over the water, especially beautiful at sunset. Riding is flat and relaxed, with little traffic away from the main roads. Fuel and food are available in Ami and the surrounding towns. The lotus fields around the lake, in bloom in summer, are a lovely sight.
t.goshikinuma@37.7,140.1:
