Goshikinuma, the Five-Colour Ponds, are a cluster of small lakes in the Urabandai highlands of Fukushima Prefecture, and their story begins with a violent morning. In 1888 Mount Bandai erupted and its northern flank collapsed in a huge landslide, burying villages and damming rivers. The water that backed up behind the debris formed hundreds of lakes and ponds, among them the large lakes of Hibara, Onogawa and Akimoto. Goshikinuma is one of the smaller results of that disaster, and today the place is peaceful beyond belief.

The ponds are known for their colours, which range from emerald to cobalt to a milky turquoise, depending on minerals, depth, light and the season. A nature trail of a few kilometres winds around them through beech and larch forest, boardwalks crossing wetland, and it is a gentle walk even in riding boots, though a lighter shoe makes it more pleasant. Autumn is the standout, when the foliage reflects in the water; in early summer fresh green dominates, and in winter the area is deep in snow.

The riding around here is part of the Bandai highland roads, with moderate climbs, smooth bends and forest on both sides. The surface is usually good, and traffic is light except in peak colour season, when cars queue at the viewpoints. Weather moves quickly in these hills: mist can drift off the lakes, and a bright morning can turn cold by afternoon. Take care in autumn when wet leaves can make corners slick, and be alert for wildlife, as Japanese black bears live in the region, though they generally avoid people.

For supplies, Inawashiro, around ten kilometres away, is the most convenient bigger town, with fuel stations and food, and Kitakata, known for its ramen, is a little farther. In the highlands, cafes and souvenir shops near the trailhead sell hot drinks and local snacks, and the area is known for buckwheat noodles. Go early, before the tour groups arrive, and the ponds are so still that the reflection looks more real than the trees.
t.lake hibara@37.7,140.1:
Lake Hibara is the largest of the lakes in the Urabandai area, and like its neighbours it is a child of 1888. That year Mount Bandai blew out its north face, sending a mass of rock and mud down the valley and blocking the Nagase river, which flooded the land behind the dam. The result is a long, irregular lake with many arms and inlets, drowned valleys that give it a ragged, complex shoreline. The volcano itself still looms above, with its broken crater wall plainly visible from the right angle.

For a rider, the lake is the centrepiece of a very enjoyable region. Roads run along its shores and over the surrounding ridges, with views opening between trees, and some are part of toll routes that link the Bandai highlands. The curves are easy and flowing rather than technical, and the surface is generally smooth, which makes this a good place for a relaxed day. Take care in autumn, when damp leaves collect in the bends, and on cool mornings when mist rises from the water and reduces visibility.

The lake is also a working landscape. Anglers fish for smelt, called wakasagi, through the ice in winter, and pleasure boats and kayaks appear in summer. The surrounding hills are forested with beech and conifers, and in October the colours are famous, drawing crowds to the viewpoints and slowing traffic. Early mornings give calmer water and fewer people, and the light on the far shore can be extraordinarily clear. Spring brings pale green and the last snow on the high slopes.

Inawashiro, with around seventeen thousand people, is the nearest large town, about fourteen kilometres away, with fuel and plenty of food, and Kitakata to the west is a similar distance. Around the lake, small shops and lodges sell refreshments, and hot-spring inns offer a bath and a meal for a night. The area is bear country, so keep noise and sensible habits when walking, and treat the quiet shores with the respect that a place with such a violent past deserves.
t.near kashima shi@36.0,140.6:
Kashima's great shrine claims to be one of the oldest in Japan, and its deity, Takemikazuchi, is a god of thunder and swords. A stone in the shrine forest, the kaname-ishi, is said to pin down the head of a giant catfish beneath the earth whose thrashing causes earthquakes. Only a small rounded top shows above ground; legend says that no amount of digging has ever reached its bottom. The forest around the shrine, with tall cedars, deer and a spring-fed pond, is a cool, dark refuge on a summer day.

The town itself is a mix of industry and sport. A huge steelworks and petrochemical complex dominates the coast, built around a deep artificial harbour, and the Kashima Antlers, one of the most successful clubs in Japanese football, play at a stadium on the edge of town.

To the east, the Kashima-nada coast runs for tens of kilometres, a long, straight beach of sand and surf facing the open Pacific. Swimming is popular in July and August, when designated beaches open with lifeguards, but the waves can be powerful and rip currents strong. Outside the official season, the beaches are the domain of surfers and fishermen.

West of the town, the shores of Kitaura and the wider Kasumigaura lake system offer flat, quiet roads through rice fields and lotus ponds. In summer the lotus flowers bloom, and herons stalk the paddies.

The approach street to the shrine has old tea houses selling sweet dumplings, which is the civilised way to take a break; for fuel and a cold can, the national road through town has the usual stations and konbini.
t.near ohara@35.2,140.4:
Every September the men of Ōhara carry portable shrines straight into the Pacific, running through the surf to the beat of drums in a festival that has been held for centuries. It is a wild, joyful sight, and it sums up this small fishing town on the eastern coast of the Boso peninsula, where life still revolves around the sea and the boats.

Ōhara is part of Isumi city, and its harbour lands some of the largest catches of Japanese spiny lobster, ise-ebi, in the country. In season, the restaurants near the port serve it grilled, boiled or in miso soup, along with whatever else the boats brought in that morning. It is a good place to eat, and lunch here is reason enough to stop.

The Isumi railway, a little single-track local line, runs inland from Ōhara through rice fields and wooded hills. In spring, rapeseed flowers bloom along the tracks, and the small yellow trains pass through a sea of colour. Railway fans travel from all over Japan to photograph it.

The coast road south towards Katsuura is a pleasant ride, with views over rocky bays and small beaches, and Katsuura's morning market, one of the most famous in Japan, has been held for over four hundred years. Inland, the roads wind through quiet valleys with little traffic, and the hills are green and wooded.

The town covers the basics, pumps and konbini included. Beaches along this stretch open for swimming in July and August, but the Pacific does not do gentle here; stay between the flags and leave the reef edges to the surfers.
